items.title: How Anthropic’s Dynamic Workflows Coordinate Claude Agents
items.summary: At AI Engineer New York, Anthropic drew on lessons from Unix and Linux to explain how agents can tackle bigger projects without overwhelming developers.
items.full_text: CJ Avilla and Harrison Stall, Members of Technical Staff at Anthropic, at AI Engineer NYC today. The AI Engineer New York 2026 conference kicked off this morning with a series of workshops, including Anthropic discussing how to orchestrate its Claude Managed Agents . Of particular interest was a brand new feature, announced on Friday , called dynamic workflows — or simply “flows,” as the presenters repeatedly called it. Flows are defined as “a new type of multiagent orchestration, built for your most ambitious workloads.” CJ Avilla and Harrison Stall , both Members of Technical Staff at Anthropic , began by invoking some operating system projects of the past — from Ken Thompson building the original Unix operating system, through to Linux evolving from one person (Linus Torvalds) to layers of trusted maintainers . The lesson: agents need the same level of organization in order to do the types of big, ambitious projects Anthropic envisions for dynamic workflows. Sponsored by Union.ai Build a sovereign AI factory The best engineering teams are building AI factories where they own and control not only their data, compute, and infrastructure, but also a durable runtime on their cloud. Union.ai gives your workflows the durability to adapt and right-size infra resources and recover from failures without re-running completed work. Get started directly through AWS Marketplace and try Union.ai free for 30 days . To learn more, visit us at AI Engineer New York booth #48. “I think a lot of us who are orchestrating and managing lots of agents now might start to feel this feeling of being the bottleneck and being the breaking point as we have lots of agents contributing tons and tons of PRs,” Avilla said. “And we’re sitting there in our GitHub trying to approve PRs and make sure that everything works as expected.” The pair noted that dynamic workflows began in Claude Code as the “a harness for every task” concept. But flows can run longer than a single agent or a roster. The basic idea is that Claude chooses the organization of agents. “Flows are essentially the next version of multi-agent orchestration,” said Stall, “where you can let Claude fully orchestrate the entirety of its own multi-agent topology.” The way this works is that the lead agent creates a plan for how it wants to accomplish tasks. Claude then writes an orchestration program, which launches agents, collects results, and manages information flow. Previously, Claude Managed Agents required developers to configure a coordinator and a roster of subagents. With dynamic workflows, Claude itself determines how to divide and orchestrate the work. “Across multiple different phases of the multi-agent orchestration, it’s able to accomplish discrete, verifiable units of work without you having to manage any of the interconnections between these things,” Stall said. That said, Avilla noted that the user can introduce specialist sub-agents if they wish. “It’s also possible in the agent config to pass in pre-configured sub-agents,” he said. All of this is available in Claude Console , the interface used by developers accessing Claude through API — the whole point of Claude Managed Agents. Claude Console, where Managed Agents is located. The presenters then showed a relatively simple workflow of a stock watchlist scanner. Although this was far removed from the big, ambitious projects Anthropic is encouraging, it did illustrate the basic pattern : a scan phase distributed individual tickers to agents with isolated contexts , and a later review phase examined the findings before producing a report. The audience Q&A surfaced a number of potential problems. One audience member asked how Claude decides how many agents a task needs , and could a simple ticker scan trigger hundreds of sub-agents? “The answer really is evals and lower defaults ,” Stall replied, noting that ambitious tasks generally require explicitly encouraging greater parallelization. One enduring concern with agent orchestration is maintaining control over your token budget . Someone asked whether the lead agent knows how much money it has available? Stall replied that the model does not know its budget while running, but that developers can set a session budget. He added that informing models of their budgets could make the agents “a little bit anxious,” which elicited chuckles from the audience. Scanner in the stock watchlist example. A related question was how can developers make repeated flows cheaper and more efficient over time? Outside of asking Claude to examine the costs incurred, Avilla suggested another relatively new feature be used: dreaming . In the documentation , “dreaming” is defined as a research preview feature. A dream “reads an existing memory store alongside past session transcripts, then produces a new, reorganized memory store, ” with duplicates merged, “stale or contradicted entries” replaced, and “new insights surfaced.” Avilla described dreaming in the flow context as being able to “crystallize and basically improve the memory store that is related to those sessions.” For the stock watchlist example, someone asked whether the watchlist flow can improve itself? For example, recognize that its scanning model is inadequate and change the next scheduled run? Stall said this wasn’t built in, but he and Avilla suggested hill-climbing and dreaming could be used to improve the loop. The brain/hands conceptual overview of Managed Agents. What about visibility into the actions of the sub-agents , another audience member asked. Avilla replied that yes, developers can always inspect that through graphing functionality inside Claude Console. “You can tell, what did the lead agent actually pass to the sub-agent? You can look at that payload here to deeply understand what is actually happening for every transition in this entire graph.” Another interesting question was whether the subagents can communicate with each other? Stall said the agents share a filesystem and can use it to exchange information, but developers cannot directly instruct one workflow subagent to message another through the API. In the watchlist-scanner comparison, Avilla said flows cost “much more” than a single-agent approach, but were also “much more effective at finding all of the details.” The bigger question is how ambitious can flows be, really? One audience member asked whether dynamic workflows can power large scientific research projects, referencing OpenAI’s recently announced proof concerning the Navier–Stokes Millennium Prize problem . While Stall wouldn’t be drawn on specifics about how Anthropic computes large scientific problems, he said it is their goal to enable general users to tackle those problems too. “Flows are basically a way to throw test-time compute at hard problems and get more capability faster out of the models,” he said. “We think, especially as an API service, that unlocking the power of this is the first step for us making these types of discoveries, or scientific progress, broadly doable by the general public. ”

items.title: Hello Python 3.15, goodbye 3.10, and now I can use 3.11
items.summary: Python 3.15 is here ! Here's the essential What's new in Python 3.15 guide, this year curated by 3.14 and 3.15 release manager Hugo van Kemenade. As someone who builds open source software that works in every supported Python version, I get to say goodbye to Python 3.10 and start embracing features from Python 3.11. First, some highlights from Python 3.15. Explicit lazy imports I'm most excited about Explicit lazy imports from PEP 810 . These let you import modules like so: lazy import json lazy from pathlib import Path The module will then be imported the first time those symbols are used in the code that follows. My LLM CLI tool implements plugins. I had to recommend manual lazy imports in the plugin author documentation, because simply installing plugins that used heavy dependencies such as sentence_transformers could add multiple seconds to every invocation of the llm command. Lazy imports directly address this startup cost. Unpacking in comprehensions The new [*sublist for sublist in lists] unpacking syntax is neat. Here's an illustration lifted from the documentation : lists = [[ 1 , 2 ], [ 3 , 4 ], [ 5 ]] [ * L for L in lists ] # [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] # equivalent to [x for L in lists for x in L] sets = [{ 1 , 2 }, { 2 , 3 }, { 3 , 4 }] { * s for s in sets } # {1, 2, 3, 4} # equivalent to {x for s in sets for x in s} dicts = [{ 'a' : 1 }, { 'b' : 2 }, { 'a' : 3 }] { ** d for d in dicts } # {'a': 3, 'b': 2} # equivalent to {k: v for d in dicts for k,v in d.items()} PEP 798: Unpacking in Comprehensions by Adam Hartz and Erik Demaine proposed this as an extension of the unpacking syntax from PEP 448 , which landed in Python 3.5 back in 2015. A sampling profiler Python's existing tracing profiler has been renamed from cProfile to profiling.tracing , and has been joined by an exciting new sampling profiler called Tachyon, aka profiling.sampling . Sampling profilers work by periodically capturing stack traces from running processes, then using those to calculate which functions have the most time spent inside of them. They're very low overhead and can provide a deep insight into running systems, without needing to instrument those systems first. I've previously used tools like py-spy for this. Now this capability is baked into the standard library. If you have the PID of an existing Python 3.15 process you can start gathering samples by running this (I had to use sudo on macOS): sudo uv run --python 3.15 python -m profiling.sampling attach 1234 Interact with the main program a bit, then hit Ctrl+C to stop gathering and see a report, which looks something like this: It can also produce flame graphs like this and heat maps like this , and can even output a format that can be viewed in the Firefox profiler UI. 3.15 isn't much faster than 3.14 Miguel Grinberg investigated How fast is Python 3.15? the other day against the 3.15.0rc3 release and found performance to be mostly the same as 3.14, with the exception of the experimental JIT. The JIT gave a 1.2x boost over the standard 3.15 interpreter (on a Fibonacci test), the first time Miguel observed a meaningful JIT performance increase. Miguel's explorations of 3.14 last year found significant boosts against Python 3.13 across many more categories. Upgrading to Python 3.15 with uv I used the following sequence of commands to get uv to use Python 3.15 on my Mac. First I had to upgrade uv itself to ensure it knew about the new release: uv self update Then I installed the stable 3.15 release: uv python install 3.15 And told uv that I wanted that to be the default for every uv run command, unless the project itself pinned a different version: uv python pin --global 3.15 Now the following reports 3.15 as the version: uv run python --version I already have a bunch of tools installed using uv tool install . I reinstalled them to use Python 3.15 like this: uv tool upgrade datasette --python 3.15 Then I can confirm the version like this: datasette --get /-/versions.json | jq Highlights from Python 3.11 The release of 3.15 means that Python 3.10 (released in 2021) is officially no longer supported . My policy for my main open source projects is to keep them working in every supported Python version. I can now drop 3.10 and start using features that were introduced in 3.11. Here's the What's new in Python 3.11 document. I finally get to rely on tomllib being available! Datasette makes extensive use of asyncio . 3.11 adds TaskGroup and timeout() , and several more new features. datetime.UTC is a new in 3.11 alias for datetime.timezone.utc . Python's SQLite support got some significant upgrades in 3.11, including: setlimit() and getlimit() expose a mechanism for setting SQLite runtime limits from Python. create_window_function() lets us create custom window functions in Python, as a class with step() , value() , inverse() , and finalize() methods. blobopen() provides an efficient mechanism for partial reads and writes of large BLOB binary values stored in a SQLite row. You can now call set_authorizer(None) to remove a SQLite authorizer. Datasette had a workaround for this! Plus a whole bunch of improvements to Python's typing system . I plan to land Python 3.11 improvements to a bunch of my projects over the next few weeks. Here's my first Datasette PR removing that set_authorizer(None) workaround. I've also updated my click-app , datasette-plugin , python-lib , and llm-plugin cookiecutter templates to test against Python 3.11 through Python 3.15. Tags: open-source , profiling , python , sqlite , uv

items.title: Applying technology to understand and treat disease
items.summary: A healthcare professional sits at a desk reviewing mammogram scans and medical diagrams on dual computer monitors.
items.full_text: Google’s health research and tools span from fundamental cellular discovery to laboratory analysis and patient impact. Over the last five years, Google teams have published 90 peer-reviewed research papers about understanding and addressing diseases, accumulating more than 90,000 citations. And building on our vision for how technology can accelerate science to improve lives , we’re collaborating with clinicians, academic institutes, and researchers to ensure discoveries make it out of the lab to benefit patients. Here is how our efforts are helping to advance medical research and public health solutions. Decoding the mechanics of disease AlphaGenome Atlas is the most comprehensive catalog of predictions for how single-letter variant changes in the human genome affect molecular biology. To effectively treat an illness, it helps to understand how it operates at the molecular, genetic, and cellular levels. Our early-stage biology models act as collaborative research tools for scientists, revealing nature's hidden mechanics and advancing medical discoveries. Accelerating drug discovery: Researchers at the Institute for Global Health, Barcelona, used AlphaFold to virtually screen 30,000 compounds for antiparasitic activity against Chagas disease, a neglected tropical illness that affects roughly 8 million people and can lead to life-threatening complications if left untreated. This research helped the Institute identify two FDA-approved drugs that could be repurposed for Chagas, expediting time-to-treatment. Mapping genetic variants linked to aging: Identifying which rare genetic changes are linked to specific diseases is challenging because the volume of non-impactful mutations creates "background noise." Researchers at the University of Exeter used AlphaGenome Atlas to search through genomic data from over 54,000 individuals, pinpointing specific variants that drive the abundance of critical proteins circulating in the human body, including PLA2G7 (linked to aging) and EGLN1 (a vital cellular oxygen sensor). Reconstructing the brain at nanoscale: In partnership with Harvard’s Lichtman Lab, we reconstructed a human brain fragment at nanoscale resolution and made the data openly available via Neuroglancer . We additionally mapped the brains of model organisms including the fly , larval zebrafish , and songbird . These neural mapping resources enable researchers to advance their study of brain function. Accelerating tools for medical solutions Visual map of proteins developed with the support of AlphaFold. The lab is where biological discovery is validated, engineered, and turned into potential medical and public health solutions. Our models have replaced slow, iterative processes with systems that can process large amounts of data quickly and accurately. Supporting genetic diagnoses with ultrarapid genome sequencing: In collaboration with Stanford University School of Medicine, we used DeepVariant and DeepConsensus in a clinical trial to help determine the cause of genetic disease in time-critical cases. The program assisted in enabling life-saving interventions by achieving genetic diagnosis with whole genome sequencing in less than eight hours, an unprecedented achievement also recognized with a Guinness World Record . Designing custom enzymes from scratch: We introduced AlphaProtein Novo , a machine learning pipeline for creating new-to-nature enzymes from first principles. In lab tests, it successfully designed custom enzymes to synthesize key drug motifs, and others to degrade toxic environmental plastics under extreme conditions — demonstrating the ability to design functional proteins that can go beyond what is currently known in nature. Supporting proactive public health initiatives: A community's health is deeply connected to its geography. We are using our Google Earth AI models in combination with environmental, weather, mobility, and other data to help public health leaders forecast disease outbreaks and deliver care to vulnerable communities. In new research from WHO AFRO and the DRC’s INRB , conversational geospatial models replaced weeks of manual coding to help identify Ebola exposure and transmission risks sooner — allowing local responders to proactively deploy mobile laboratories. Supporting medical providers with machine learning models New mammography screening systems can help to catch historically missed interval cancers and reduce specialist reading workloads. A medical breakthrough only matters if it can help real people. Our research demonstrates that machine learning models can help support disease detection as well as alleviate the administrative workload so providers can focus on care. Flagging historically missed cancer signatures: In a pair of studies published in Nature Cancer in collaboration with Imperial College London and the UK’s National Health Service (NHS), we evaluated a mammography screening system across 125,000 women. The system caught 25% of historically missed interval cancers while showing the possibility of reducing specialist reading workloads by up to 40% — which could help provide crucial relief to healthcare systems facing severe radiologist shortages. Uncovering hidden pediatric leukemia mutations: When applied by Children’s Mercy Hospital to previously sequenced real-world childhood leukemia cases, DeepSomatic confirmed all known variants while detecting 10 previously missed mutations — despite the challenge of working with a tumor-only sample. DeepSomatic is publicly available and has the potential to inform clinical judgments around patient risk and targeted treatments. Predicting global flu surges: A Google flu forecasting model was ranked #1 by the Centers for Disease Control (CDC) for predicting flu-related hospital admissions during the 2025–2026 season. Developed using our Empirical Research Assistance tool, the model outperformed 38 other systems to accurately match observed hospitalizations, showing how the technology can help public health officials anticipate demand for medical services and better prepare for seasonal outbreaks. Better health within reach for everyone Transforming health requires scientists, researchers, and institutions working hand-in-hand. That’s why we equip the science community with the advanced models and open-access platforms to fuel breakthrough research — along with the philanthropic funding and computing power they need to apply that research. Through Google.org, we’re supporting organizations like the Infectious Disease Institute at Makerere University to forecast malaria drug resistance mutations with AlphaFold and AlphaMissense, and the University of Pennsylvania, using AlphaProteo and AlphaFold to help design novel cellular therapies that can augment the treatment of solid tumors and complex diseases. In 2026, Google.org has provided over $60 million to organizations around the world that are applying advanced models to transform how we understand and treat diseases. By meeting disease at every stage, we can turn the most intractable human health challenges into actionable solutions, helping people everywhere live longer, healthier lives.

items.title: web-edit 0.1a0
items.summary: Release: web-edit 0.1a0 I was working on a project from my phone using Codex Remote when I found myself wanting to edit a credentials file without round-tripping those credentials through the LLM itself. So... I had Codex and GPT-6 Astra Extra High build this Python web app which provides a web UI for viewing and editing files in a folder. It's intended to be run over Tailscale, so I can have an agent start this running and then edit files via my Tailscale network directly from my phone. Here's the interface for browsing files in a folder: Editing uses CodeMirror 6 - I was going to use Monaco but that still doesn't have a great mobile experience yet. Tags: projects , python , ai , tailscale , generative-ai , llms , codex

items.title: Dwarf Fortress uses version control now
items.summary: I remember hearing a while ago that Dwarf Fortress didn't use version control. That fact has been lodged in my head, because given its inherent complexity I have trouble imagining a codebase that would benefit from version control more . That's art. I went looking and I'm sad to report that the days without version control appear to have ended. Quoting Tarn Adams over time: March 2013: "I don't use version control -- I didn't like the feeling of having the code get committed into a black box thingy with no immediate upside" March 2016: "I don’t even use version control. If you don’t know what that is then you’re not gonna yell at me. If you even know what version control is you’re gonna be like, ‘You don’t use version control? You don’t use source control? What is wrong with you? How can you even work? I’m just not cut out for it, in a sense. It’s been 15 years, so the reasons have change over time, but that’s my current understanding of it." March 2023: "I've got Discord channels to check and version control stuff to use now, so the process is definitely a little more involved" That March 2023 quote comes from an interview about the release on Steam which made them millionaires . I'm a tiny bit sad that they gave in before they hit that milestone, but what an impressive run. Tags: version-control

items.title: Building AI for Reliable Execution: Lessons From Industrial Robotics
items.summary: Inside Standard Bots’ AI stack, pretrained models learn factory tasks from demonstrations and improve through corrections from real deployments.
items.full_text: When you think of robotics and AI, you probably first think of full humanoid robots like Figure’s AI-powered machines and 1X’s NEO home robots . Those may well be the future, but arguably more important in 2026 is industrial robots — which are typically not humanoids. Standard Bots claims to be “America’s largest AI-native industrial robot manufacturer.” It recently raised $200 million at a $1 billion valuation, in a series C round led by General Catalyst and RoboStrategy, a fund focused on robotics. Its customers include NASA, Amazon and Lockheed Martin. We spoke to Evan Beard , co-founder and CEO, and Leif Jentoft , Head of AI, to find out more about Standard Bots’ AI stack and how its models work. To set the scene, Standard Bots’ industrial robot arms are designed for tasks such as machine tending, welding, and assembly. Here’s a quick demo by Jentoft: According to Beard, Standard Bots has a shared base model that customers adapt through demonstrations and fine-tuning. Jentoft added that Standard Bots runs a range of models , including a zero-shot perception system for machine tending. Beard says its largest model is in the low billions of parameters — so it’s not that large by frontier lab standards. “We believe data quality matters far more than raw volume,” said Jentoft, “and we focus on getting the most out of targeted data rather than chasing the largest possible dataset.” (This matches the “bitterest lesson” of Jev creator Diogo Almeida , who told us recently that the right task and the right data can matter more than compute.) “Our market access gives us unique access to the highest value data,” he added. “ In-situ interventions can fix an edge case with a few dozen examples.” Setting up part identification with ClickFind. Beard notes that Standard Bots focuses on short-horizon tasks to meet production requirements for cycle time and reliability. The company uses conventional programming for parts of a workflow that don’t require learned behavior. Model training happens in the cloud but inference runs locally , said Beard. I asked Jentoft what the learned model does in a typical robot routine, and which parts of the workflow use conventional programming? As an example, he brought up its machine-tending solution for high-mix manufacturing. “We’ve built a zero-shot system that lets a user tell the robot which parts to look for on a given task. The model handles perception — locating and identifying the parts — while conventional programming handles the motion and the cell logic around it.” Here’s a demonstration of the machine-tending: “Our backbone for this task is trained on over a billion images , which is what lets the robot distinguish between lighting conditions, material types, and an object versus its background,” Jentoft said. Back in April, we had Applied Intuition on the podcast to talk about “Physical AI” and how it differs from on-screen AI. One of the learnings was that the Physical AI isn’t just constrained by model intelligence: the hard part is deploying models onto real hardware , under safety, latency, power, cost, and reliability constraints. But for Standard Bots, that can also be a strength, since it controls the “full stack” from software to hardware. Jentoft points out that it controls the robotic arm, end effector, control system, and AI. “That lets us co-optimize the models and the control policies ,” he said. “Despite claims elsewhere, no model today is truly hardware-agnostic, and co-optimizing low-level control and higher-level functions is a major advantage for both performance and iteration speed.” Skild , a company aiming to build “general purpose robotic intelligence,” might quibble with the hardware-agnostic claim — its goal is to achieve cross-hardware generalization . Beard had mentioned that inference is done locally, which is especially important for its core customers: factories. “For factories, which is most of what we’re doing right now — and certainly so much opportunity that we see there — this is something where you need to do inference on-premise ,” he said. An AI agent building a machine-tending routine. For machine tending, the model identifies parts while conventional programming handles motion. Jentoft also described how models can generate actions that feed into the robot’s control system. “Wrist cameras and other sensors feed raw pixels and signals into the system over internal gigabit Ethernet , routed internally so no cables tangle,” he explained. “ GPUs at the edge process that data to generate action chunks , which stream to low-level control.” He reiterated that inference is run on-premises deliberately. “Cloud compute for robotics is operationally extremely hard — most factories and warehouses don’t have reliable internet , and that’s even more true for mobile robots. Uptime is crucial to customer acceptance, so we keep the loop local.” Standard Bots uses simulation where it can, but Beard says some production tasks — including those involving liquids, suction, or cutting flexible material — are difficult to reproduce in current simulators. Real-world demonstrations are another part of the learning process. Here’s a demo of teaching a robot using a handheld touch device: So how does it deal with failure in a robot task, and do those kinds of learnings flow back to the model? “We capture failure signals and human corrections from deployments, and how we use that data depends on the customer,” Jentoft replied. He noted that many of its defense customers “deploy in air-gapped environments, where nothing comes back.” But for customers that aren’t air-gapped, “fleet learning delivers enough benefit to their own applications that we typically don’t see pushback on contributing data in exchange for that performance.” Standard Bots has already expanded its platform so that external developers can use it. With StandardOS , it offers a set of APIs and SDKs. According to Beard, developers can use Standard Bots’ APIs to build robotics applications with whichever parts of its stack they need, including bringing their own models. He cited NVIDIA Cosmos , an open family of omnimodal world models for physical AI, as an example ( version 3 was released late-May ). Today, this requires developers to write their own integration code. But Standard Bots plans to make collecting data, training models, and deploying them onto its robots easier. AI robot learning workflow with NVIDIA software; via Standard Bots. Standard Bots isn’t the sexiest robotics company out there, but it is already being deployed for industrial automation at NASA, Amazon, Lockheed Martin, and others. For AI engineers, perhaps the most useful lesson is how Standard Bots adapts AI to a specific job. It keeps the model’s role focused and uses corrections from real deployments to fix edge cases. You can, of course, apply that same approach to software agents. As Jentoft said — and it was a recent lesson from Jev too — it’s all about “getting the most out of targeted data rather than chasing the largest possible dataset.”

items.title: [AINews] TypeSafe/Jev at >$100M ARR, $7.5B valuation 3 weeks after launch
items.summary: Wow.
items.full_text: As you can see in the AINews X recap section below, everyone on earth has cloned the Jev API, but only one company can ever create the category. TypeSafe announced their “ Series AI ” and Sequoia “ leaked ” that they crossed 100M ARR in their first week. Diogo Almeida @CompleteSkeptic launched a model accidentally served trillions of tokens a day 29.4% of the fortune 500 showed up raised a really big series A from it's been 3 weeks we would like to sleep now 4:26 PM · Oct 9, 2026 · 811K Views 467 Replies · 219 Reposts · 6.07K Likes Although there are cynics and accusations of astroturfing , we hope it is evident that our Jev pod was 100% authentic. AI News for 10/8/2026-10/9/2026. We checked 12 subreddits, 544 Twitters and no further Discords. AINews’ website lets you search all past issues. As a reminder, AINews is now a section of Latent Space . You can opt in/out of email frequencies! Decision Models Become a Product Category The pattern : Several vendors shipped “decision” models on the same day. These return typed answers (probabilities, picks from a list, scores) in a single forward pass instead of free text. Jev is the reference point everyone benchmarks against, and @scaling01 remarked on how fast the format spread. OpenAI Decisions API : Three request types: probability that a condition is true, pick from a list, or score against levels. It accepts text and images, runs on GPT-6 Luna, costs $0.10/M input tokens with no output charge, and is “up to 10x faster” by OpenAI’s own figure ( @LearnOpenCV ). Microsoft-Decision-1 : Positioned for LLM judges and screening scientific hypotheses. An early evaluator says decision models still struggle on consistency and complex decisions ( @omarsar0 ). Perplexity pplx-decider-v1.1-27b : Claims top Decision Bench accuracy at 94.5% across 1,071 cases, at $0.017 per 1K decisions ( @perplexitydevs ). Cloudflare clef : New clef-omni accepts audio, video, image and text. clef-flash is now cheaper than Jev, and clef overall is about 2x faster ( @michellechen ). Weights are on Hugging Face . Liquid d1 : Now on Vercel AI Gateway, with vision support for classify, route and score tasks ( @vercel_dev ). Serving and routing : vLLM Semantic Router’s Decision 2.0 answers multiple questions about one input in one pass, with per-option probabilities ( @vllm_project ). LangSmith uses Jev as a judge that returns separate typed answers for difficulty and correctness on every trace ( @hwchase17 ). Train your own : Unsloth released a free notebook that turns Qwen3.5-4B into a decision model on 8GB of VRAM ( @UnslothAI ). A walkthrough on Qwen3.5-0.8B reports accuracy rising from 37% to 65% in 60 steps, about 10 minutes on 4GB ( @akshay_pachaar ). Why harnesses want this : Many agent steps are yes/no calls rather than generation. LangChain says routing each task to the cheapest adequate model cut median Open SWE cost per task by 64% ( @hwchase17 ). Related research : Apple/CMU’s Selection-based Structured Reasoning (SSR) applies the same idea inside agents ( @ZhihuFrontier ). Method : Six natural-language strategies are scored by length-normalized log-likelihood in one batched forward pass that shares the KV cache. Results : Per-turn reasoning latency falls by more than 90%, but end-to-end latency per question falls only 28–54%. On Qwen3-VL-4B with GRPO, average success is 61.37% versus 61.25% for a TAPO+GSPO baseline. Multi-Agent Orchestration and Coding Tools Claude Managed Agents dynamic workflows (public beta) : A lead agent writes a phased plan, fans it out to up to 1,000 agents per run, then merges the results. It is enabled with multiagent_20261001 ( @ClaudeDevs , config ). Cost warning : Anthropic advises starting with scoped tasks because token use can be high ( guidance ). Claude Code Projects : All waitlisted Pro and Max users were admitted. Each project runs tasks as parallel threads ( @ClaudeDevs ), and sessions can now run locally ( @gem_ray ). Opus 5.5 fast mode : It has rolled out, but it bills against usage credits and is not included in subscriptions ( @theo ). Do agent teams pay off? : Vals AI ran GPT-6 Sol and Opus 5.5 on Vibe Code Bench, alone and as teams ( @ValsAI ). Results : Teams cost 1.8–5.1x more. Only Sol at medium effort improved significantly, by 7.3 points. Behavior : Sol delegated in parallel along architectural lines. Opus ran sequential waves, reaching about 6.8 subagents and roughly 1,140 subagent tool calls per app at max effort, with no significant gain ( details ). Prime Agent rewrites itself in Rust : Over two weeks, a swarm of more than 2,000 agents used 10K+ sandboxes and 200B+ GLM-5.3 tokens. The result reaches usable input about 13x faster and uses 83% less startup memory ( @PrimeIntellect ). An accompanying essay argues that context limits lead inevitably to swarms ( essay ). Codex updates : Windows sandbox : A new mode built on Microsoft Execution Containers (MXC) gives faster setup, network enforcement and granular file controls ( @OpenAIDevs ). Composer predictions : Codex now suggests your next message, in beta for Pro users only ( announcement ). Some users criticize the Pro-only gating ( @Angaisb_ ). Reliability : There were complaints of daylong outages ( @dzhng ). Sentiment : DHH says GPT-6.1 Sol made Codex his primary tool over Claude ( @dhh ). Devin and Grok Bot : Devins can now spawn trees of managed Devins, so wall time tracks the slowest branch rather than the sum ( @devindevelopers ). Devin also accepts personal ChatGPT plans for GPT usage ( @cognition ). Separately, Grok Bot gets its own email address for sign-ups and scheduling ( @bot ). Model Releases and Independent Evals Qwen-Image-2.1-Turbo (open weights) : An accelerated checkpoint of the 7B Qwen-Image-2.1. It does 8-step 2K generation and natural-language editing, loads through Diffusers QwenImage21Pipeline , and launches alongside Pro and Turbo APIs ( @Alibaba_Qwen ). StepFun Step 5 Preview : A 600B-total, 27B-active sparse MoE with 1M context and vision ( @omarsar0 ). Results : It scores 33.89 on the Hermes Index, matching GPT-6 Luna, and is free on Nous Portal for a week ( @NousResearch ). Availability : It reached #1 on OpenRouter Trending, which measures usage, not quality ( @kimmonismus ). Open weights are due October 15. Max output was corrected to 64K tokens ( correction ). Upstage Solar Mini 4 : A 35B MoE with 3B active, 524K context and 208 tok/s. Its AAII score of 24 is the best at 3B active, within a point of Nemotron 3 Ultra. It is free in Cline ( @cline ). Gemini 4 Argon : Reported at 77.9% on DeepSWE v1.1 versus Opus 5.5’s 74.2%. It ships first to 650+ Fairwind Program defenders at $2/$10 per M tokens ( @dl_weekly ). Signals : Reasoning-effort selectors have appeared in Antigravity ( @testingcatalog ), and Logan Kilpatrick says “Argon is coming” ( @OfficialLoganK ). Unconfirmed : Business Insider reports that an internal “Carbon” checkpoint approaches Opus 5.5 on coding. Speech models : HeyGen Voice tops the Artificial Analysis Controlled Voice TTS arena with an Elo of 1,201, at $30/1M characters and 40 chars/s ( @ArtificialAnlys ). Whistle is a 16.9MB on-device STT model said to rival Whisper base ( @victormustar ). Multi-turn image editing : Artificial Analysis chained 30 consecutive edits ( @ArtificialAnlys ). Results : Ideogram 4.5 and FLUX 3 edit locally, leaving 95%+ of the image untouched on small edits. GPT Image 2.5 Sunburst re-renders most of the frame each turn, keeping only about 20% unchanged, so it drifts. Nano Banana 2.1 gradually darkens. OCR benchmarks : Roboflow’s new benchmark covers 48 models, with GPT-6 Astra leading text localization ( @skalskip92 ). Datalab’s OmniParseBench has 16K tests across 90 languages, and its own model does not rank first ( @VikParuchuri ). Arena roundup : Claude Haiku 5.5 ranks #30 on WebDev at $0.10/$0.50, matching GPT-6 Luna’s price while scoring 6 points higher. Mistral Large 4 sits at #43 on Agent Arena ( @arena ). On ARC-AGI-3, a new high score of 59.17% ( @arcprize ). Research, Training and Inference Systems vLLM and SGLang on Vera Rubin : vLLM reports more than 7.8x GB200 throughput on MiniMax M3 at matched interactivity on AgentX. These are early results ( @vllm_project ). Technique : Locality-aware MoE uses CUDA 13.4 locality domains so each SM reads only local HBM, worth up to 1.2x faster MoE decode ( details ). SGLang : Up to 20% faster FP8 MLA at 128K context, and a 5.9% end-to-end gain from MoE tail fusion that removes 276 launches per decode step ( @sgl_project ). SemiAnalysis claims : A preview InferenceX submission shows 3.2x profit per gigawatt and up to 10x performance per dollar versus GB300 ( @SemiAnalysis_ ). TRL v1.15 : The fused LM head is now on by default and avoids materializing the full logits tensor ( @LysandreJik ). Data and post-training services : Datology Curation Studio : Claims a 6x compute multiplier on 39 open datasets for a 30B MoE ( @pratyushmaini ). It also cites Thomson-1, trained for $450K, beating GPT-5.6 Sol head-to-head ( @arimorcos ). Tinker : Price cuts of up to 70%, long-context priced the same as short, and GLM-5.3-Flash and DeepSeek-v4.1-Flash added ( @tinkerapi ). DeepSeek periodic weak spots : ByteDance Seed finds that retrieval depends on where a token lands relative to the compression stride ( @ZhihuFrontier ). Evidence : The pattern persists without RoPE or learned gates, and tracks stride length. Interpretation : V4.1’s stride of 2 reduces but does not eliminate the effect. Agent research : Agent plasticity (Meta) : Measures held-out gain per learning dollar. The best performers are not the most efficient learners ( @omarsar0 ). MIMESIS : A 9B user simulator that beats Opus 5 on behavioral fidelity by 13.4 points ( @dair_ai ). Base-model selection (NVIDIA) : Ranks checkpoints by whether the base model can reproduce the “decisive edit,” a signal that tracks post-trained SWE-bench Verified scores ( @dair_ai ).
