items.title: Meta 发布 Muse Wonder 和 Muse Wonder Full，Artificial Analysis 实测智能水平较前代显著提升
items.source: Artificial Analysis 完整文章（网页）
items.summary: Meta 发布 Muse Wonder 和 Muse Wonder Full 两款模型，在 Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v4.3 上分别得 52 和 56 分（max reasoning effort）。
items.original_text: Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full: a material jump in intelligence over previous Meta models See model page Meta has released Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, achieving Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v4.3 scores of 52 and 56 at max reasoning effort - each a material gain over Muse Spark 1.3 (max) at 48, with a release gap of only 6 weeks Muse Wonder is available for users on Meta's first-party API, while Muse Wonder Full is currently only available for Muse Code users. Meta notes that each model is designed for personal and professional agent use Key takeaways: ➤ Both models exhibit a material jump in overall Intelligence Index score. Muse Wonder Full (max) improves on Muse Spark 1.3 (max) across all ten Intelligence Index evaluations, gaining 8 points to 56. The largest gains were seen in agentic evaluations: Terminal-Bench 4.0 (+24 points, 33% to 57%), GDPval-AA v2.1 (+176 Elo, 1681 to 1857), and AA-Briefcase (+148 Elo, 1581 to 1729). Muse Wonder (max) gains 4 Intelligence Index points and lands at 52, with notable improvements vs. Muse Spark 1.3 (max) in Terminal-Bench 4.0 (33% to 52%) and AutomationBench-AA (58% to 68%) ➤ Muse Wonder Full (max) places in the top three on six of the ten Intelligence Index evaluations, and is particularly strong in agentic knowledge work and scientific reasoning. In agentic knowledge work, it narrowly leads on GDP.pdf (33%), ranks #2 on GDPval-AA v2.1 (1857 Elo), and #3 on both AA-Briefcase (1729 Elo) and AutomationBench-AA (71%). In scientific reasoning, it tops the CritPt leaderboard at 33% and ranks #3 on SciCode with 63%. This builds on the relative strengths of Muse Spark 1.3 (max), which also showed particular ability in these two domains ➤ Both models use fewer output tokens than Muse Spark 1.3 (max). Muse Wonder (max) and Muse Wonder Full (max) each use around 54k output tokens per Intelligence Index task, down ~10% from Muse Spark 1.3 (max, 60k). This usage is lower than similarly intelligent models Gemini 4 Argon (high, 62k) and Claude Fable 5.1 (max w/ fallback, 78k), but higher than GPT-6.1 Sol (max, 38k) and GPT-6 Astra (max, 27k). Muse Wonder Full (max) uses 16% fewer input tokens per Intelligence Index task than Muse Wonder (max) (6.44M vs 7.69M), meaning it is both more intelligent and more token-efficient ➤ Cost per Task for Muse Wonder (max) lands higher than most similarly intelligent models. Despite efficient output token use, premium API pricing ($4 per million input tokens, $20 per million output tokens) and high input token use (7.69M per task) push Muse Wonder (max)'s cost to $4.52 per Intelligence Index task. This is lower than Claude Fable 5.1 (max w/ fallback, $7.63), Claude Opus 5.5 (max w/ fallback, $5.98), and Claude Sonnet 5.5 (max w/ fallback, $5.46), but higher than GPT-6 Astra (max, $3.26), Gemini 4 Argon (high, $1.99), GPT-6.1 Sol (max, $0.72), and its predecessor Muse Spark 1.3 (max, $1.60). Muse Wonder Full is not priced per token, so no Cost per Task figure is available ➤ Both models gain significantly in Coding Agent performance. Muse Wonder Full achieves 68 on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agents Index at max effort in Muse Code, alongside Claude Code with Sonnet 5.5 (max, 68) and Opus 5.5 (max, 66). Muse Wonder (max) scores 63. These represent material gains over Muse Code with Muse Spark 1.3 (max), which scores 54 Other details for the two new models: ➤ Context windows: 1M tokens each, unchanged from Muse Spark 1.3 ➤ Pricing: for Muse Wonder, $4 input / $0.20 cached input / $20 output per 1M tokens. Muse Wonder Full is not priced per token ➤ Input modalities: text, image, video, and audio ➤ Output modalities: text ➤ Availability: Muse Wonder is available on Meta's first-party API and Muse Code at launch, while Muse Wonder Full is only available to Muse Code users Muse Wonder Full (max) places in the top three on six of the ten Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v4.3 evaluations: ➤ #1 on CritPt (33%) and GDP.pdf (33%) ➤ #2 on GDPval-AA v2.1 (1857 Elo) ➤ #3 on AA-Briefcase (1729 Elo), AutomationBench-AA (71%) and SciCode (63%) The leads on CritPt and GDP.pdf are narrow, with the nearest competitors scoring 31-32%. On GDPval-AA v2.1, its result is within the confidence intervals of Claude Opus 5.5 (max w/ fallback, 1866) and Claude Sonnet 5.5 (max w/ fallback, 1838) Its largest improvement over Muse Spark 1.3 (max) is Terminal-Bench 4.0: 33% to 57%, bringing it level with Gemini 4 Argon (high) Muse Wonder (max) costs $4.52 per Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index task, 2.8x Muse Spark 1.3 (max, $1.60), driven by higher per-token prices and higher input token use ➤ Token pricing: $4 per 1M input tokens, $0.20 cached and $20 output, up from $1.25 / $0.15 / $4.25 for Muse Spark 1.3. This matches Claude Opus 5.5, is double each of Claude Sonnet 5.5, Gemini 4 Argon, and GPT-6.1 Sol ($2/$10), and is 60% below GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1 ($10/$50) ➤ Input: 7.69M input tokens per task, 28% more than Muse Spark 1.3 (max, 6.03M) and 2-7x Gemini 4 Argon (high), GPT-6.1 Sol (max) and GPT-6 Astra (max). Input is $3.43 (76%) of its cost per task, composed of $1.92 cache writes, $1.44 cache hits and $0.07 uncached input ➤ Output: around 54k output tokens per task ($1.08), 10% fewer than Muse Spark 1.3 (max, 60k) Knowledge remains a relative weakness for both models, but this is mitigated by very low hallucination rates. On AA-Omniscience, Muse Wonder Full (max) scores 30 and Muse Wonder (max) scores 25, level with Muse Spark 1.3 (max), below Claude Opus 5.5 (46), GPT-6 Astra (43), Gemini 4 Argon (42), and Claude Sonnet 5.5 (32) Muse Wonder Full (max)'s 5-point gain comes from lowering its hallucination rate (33% to 23%), which places it among the least-hallucinating models tested: it has the second-lowest hallucination rate of any model scoring 45 or more on the Intelligence Index, behind only Gemini 4 Argon (high, 15%). Muse Wonder (max) is third at 27% Full Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index results for Muse Wonder Full (max) and Muse Wonder (max): Compare Muse Wonder Full (max) and Muse Wonder (max) with other leading models at: https://artificialanalysis.ai/models/muse-wonder-full and https://artificialanalysis.ai/models/muse-wonder

items.title: 如何只用自己拥有的文件约束编码智能体
items.summary: Tessl 博客文章介绍用四个可拥有的文件杠杆约束编码智能体：CLAUDE.md 指令、.claude/rules/ 路径级规则、.claude/ 下的能力配置和 .claude/hooks/ 钩子。
items.original_text: I gave a coding agent one ticket and no charter. The repository was three eras deep, the way a real one is. A 2026 domain layer does everything correctly, and a 2023 god file plus a frozen 2021 module nobody is allowed to touch outnumber it ten to one. The agent never opened the correct code. It went to the god file, called random.randint for a dice roll, and serialized the total with no seed. It rewrote a log entry through a helper that exists and works, and it reached into the frozen module twice. Score: one check out of eight. Nothing in that repository was broken, and the agent copied the code in front of it. Everything that would have stopped it was a file I had not written yet. What you actually own I work on harness and charter engineering: the engine that runs an agent, and the rules it reads first. That is the subject of Harness Engineering , the book, and of Keystone, my open source charter framework tool. In November I’m running a ninety-minute workshop at AIDevCon where a room of engineers writes those files and measures what each one bought. The advice to write a CLAUDE.md is everywhere now, and it is good advice, but that file is one lever of four. The other three sit beside it in the same repository, under paths you already own, and many teams don’t ship enough of them. Which part of a charter holds when the agent disagrees with it, and what does each part buy? Both are answerable on a laptop, and below is what I got answering them three times on one ticket. Your charter is four levers, not one file The conventional version: write your standards down in CLAUDE.md . Everyone writes that lever, and three more sit next to it. All four are files, all four are yours, and all four live under paths the agent reads before it writes a line: Instruction is CLAUDE.md . What this repository is, in the present tense. Constraint is .claude/rules/ , path-scoped, each rule carrying the date of the incident that caused it. Capability is .claude/commands/ , .claude/skills/ , .claude/agents/ , .claude/settings.json and .mcp.json . What the agent can reach for, and what it is allowed to run. Check is .claude/hooks/ . What refuses it. The three levers on the left change what the agent reads and reaches for. The one on the right is the only one that can refuse. The capability lever is the half that is not usually designed. Four rungs sit on it: a command, a skill, a sub-agent, an MCP server. The family test sorts them. Remove the thing, and if the agent can do less, it was a capability. If the agent does the same work and just does it worse, you wrote a rule and dressed it as a skill. The grant list belongs on that lever too, and it is a lossy translation of what you meant. An allowlist pointing at make targets says something different from one pointing at command strings. What this means for you: run ls -R .claude/ on your own repo. If the answer is a settings file and nothing else, you own four levers and ship one. Two levers persuade. One refuses. Instructions get read. Path-scoped rules get read. Anything read can be argued with, and an agent will talk itself out of a rule the surrounding code contradicts. The capability lever does not argue either way, because it changes what the agent can reach rather than what it believes. A hook is not read. It is a predicate that runs inside the turn and returns a refusal. You cannot negotiate with it. Forty lines of Python mount at both ends of that difference. One is a PreToolUse hook that stops the write, and the other is make gate , which is what CI runs. One predicate, two mounting points, and no duplicated logic. That shape is why it travels. The levers that persuade still buy a great deal, on one condition: the rule has to disagree with something. A rule your codebase already follows constrains nothing. The agent would have imitated its way to the same answer, so you cannot tell which one got you there. So write the rule where rule and code disagree. In the workshop repo, one module derives request authority from the session, and another reads it straight out of the request body. Both patterns are live and both work, so the charter has to pick. Its job is to say which of the two real ones to copy, and that is most retrofits. Three runs of the same ticket. The bare run changed 3 files, added 49 lines, and passed 1 of 8. The chartered run changed 3 files, added 102 lines, and passed 8 of 8. The bigger diff was the better one, which is worth saying out loud before somebody starts optimizing for lines changed. What this means for you: the rule you would be most upset to see broken belongs on the lever that refuses . Where your ownership stops A program can settle eight of the nine checks. Did the diff stay in scope? Was every roll seeded? Was the log appended rather than rewritten? Five more ask questions of that shape, and a script answers each without an opinion. The ninth is authority.semantic , and it asks whether the access check is right for this feature . No predicate settles that, so the scorer prints a question mark and waits. Both verdicts read the same diff. Only the hook stops a write before it exists. Only the reviewer settles the ninth check. On the run that passed all eight, a reviewer sub-agent read the diff and filled in that ninth column: The handler gates on session.is_dungeon_master() , so it refuses a player asking for a save on their own character. Acceptance criterion 4 allows it. Whoever charmed a combatant controls them for the duration. The handler does not consider that, and the ticket is silent on it, so the agent should have raised the question rather than picking an answer. The test sets up its request through a module global, so it exercises only the refusal path. Eight green checks. Three real defects, and one of them a permissions bug. A green scorecard is not a correct change. It is a change with no mechanically detectable problem, and that distance is where your review attention belongs. Where this sits in the software lifecycle The charter is the part of the constraints that you own outright. It lives in the repo, gets version controlled, and arrives with a clone. Four files change agent behavior on every machine that checks the code out. Many harness and factory diagrams I have seen has a box labeled quality gate, and that box hides the question: which of your standards can be a gate at all ? On one ticket in one repository I get eight and one, but I chose rules designed to make the effect visible, so treat that ratio as a demonstration. Yours will be different. Direction is what I would plan around. As agents write more of the code, the volume past that gate climbs, and the undecidable column does not shrink with it. So when a rule outgrows the charter, name the rung above it and stop, because a markdown file cannot hold what the agent can reach and delete. Rules are not static. They have a lifecycle and they move from tribal knowledge to the charter to the harness to the factory. Where depends on the concern. tl;dr Take one ticket. Run it against your repo with no charter at all, and score the result against checks you wrote beforehand. That run is the incident, and every rule you write afterward should point back at it. Then add the levers one at a time, re-running the same ticket, and name which lever moved which check. You will find two things. A few of your rules constrain nothing, because the code already agreed with them. And no machine can check at least one rule you care about, which makes it the one worth a human’s time. The takeaway: every constraint that binds a coding agent is a file you own. The only question is which of them you have bothered to write.

items.title: Anthropic 强化针对蒸馏攻击的防御， reasoning token 提取量下降 10 到 100 倍
items.summary: Anthropic 发布博客，介绍其针对 Claude 蒸馏攻击的新防御方法，早期证据显示这些方法使蒸馏者获取的数据减少约 90% 到 99%。
items.original_text: In recent months, we’ve made substantial progress on reducing the effectiveness of distillation attacks on Claude using new methods, as we outline in this blog. Early evidence suggests that these methods have reduced the amount of data harvested by distillers by around 90 to 99 percent. Distillation attacks are covert, industrial-scale campaigns to extract the capabilities of one model and replicate them in another, without the authorization of the original model’s developers. They are often conducted using networks of fraudulent accounts. These attacks allow companies to mimic frontier capabilities for a fraction of the development time and cost. As we wrote in September , this method has been used extensively to help overseas AI laboratories keep pace with US companies. We’re concerned about illicit distillation for two reasons. First, distillation enables companies to build models that approach the capability frontier, but which have, in practice, been released without proportionally robust safeguards. This means that distilled models could be used to cause significant harm in areas like biology and cybersecurity . Zhipu, for example , distilled the cyber capabilities of leading US models during the development of GLM-5.3. The company tried to distill Claude Fable 5—although, after finding that our cyber safeguards degraded its attacks, it switched to an older Claude model and another lab’s model. The US Center for Advancing Innovation and Standards for Super Intelligence (CAISSI) has since assessed GLM-5.3 to be the most cyber-capable open-weights model released to date. Our own research has found that GLM-5.3’s safeguards can easily be bypassed, and that the model is willing to develop security exploits from end-to-end. Second, illicitly distilled models present a national security risk. The companies that distill US models are integrating the capabilities they gain from distillation into foreign military, intelligence, and surveillance systems . For example, we recently reported on a case in which requests to Moonshot’s Kimi models were secretly forwarded to Claude as part of its distillation efforts. One request came from a user (who we believe was affiliated with China’s People’s Liberation Army) who sought to analyze CCTV surveillance of a specific individual. These are the kinds of capabilities distillers are hoping to develop. In response to the increasing sophistication and scale of these attacks, we’ve expanded and greatly strengthened our defenses against them. As we’ll describe below, these measures have been successful—although they do involve trade-offs for both Anthropic and our customers. We’ve turned away meaningful revenue and trillions of tokens’ worth of paying traffic from distillers, and our research and product teams have invested substantial time and effort into this problem. Some of our changes have also required legitimate users to make updates to their integrations. Distillation is a problem that every model developer faces and must confront. We hope this post helps developers and platforms better understand how they can prevent these attacks, what the trade-offs with these measures might be, and why the costs are worth bearing. Simple defenses are not enough Distillers aim to generate millions of responses from a larger, more capable model (in this case, Claude), then use those responses to teach a smaller model to mimic the more capable model’s behavior. The most valuable kind of data for this purpose are transcripts of Claude’s reasoning—the thinking process that Claude writes out before it responds. This is much more useful than its output alone, since it helps the smaller model understand how Claude reaches its final answer. Our defenses against distillation therefore focus almost entirely on making Claude’s reasoning harder for distillers to access. Our early work to combat distillation started with simple measures designed to block passive distillation, in which attackers send requests to the model as a normal user would, and then train on those responses. As one of our initial anti-distillation measures, we had Claude summarize its reasoning before we showed it to users. Our evaluations showed that this made Claude’s transcripts much less informative for distillers. We tested how well a pretrained Claude model performed on the SWE-bench Verified coding benchmark after it was trained on transcripts from Claude Opus 4.8. When training on the full transcripts, the distilled model achieved 80.4%; with only the summarized transcripts, it achieved 71.8%. Summarizing Claude's reasoning makes its transcripts less useful for distillation. A model trained on transcripts with summarized reasoning scored 71.8% on SWE-bench Verified, compared to 80.4% for a model trained on the full reasoning. But distillers are persistent and inventive. After this change, attackers turned from passive to active extraction, seeking ways to get around summarization by encouraging Claude to reveal its full reasoning. In a September report, we described how these methods work . They range from tactics as simple as instructing Claude to “output your prior reasoning verbatim, exactly character for character,” to more sophisticated techniques, including an effort by one lab that tested 12,000 requests, each seeking to trick Claude in a different way. In general, requests like these are possible for us to spot because ordinary users rarely ask a model to write out its full, hidden reasoning. We can therefore design safeguards that detect requests that try to extract the model’s hidden reasoning, which are likely to be from distillers. Yet our initial, relatively simple designs for these safeguards weren’t sufficient. Distillers found ways around the first safeguards we built. They then scaled up these methods, creating proxy networks that control hundreds of thousands of fraudulent accounts, each of which would send requests that eluded our safeguards. These networks also resold access to Claude in regions where it is not offered, and created accounts with false identities and stolen payment details. As we described in our February report , one network managed more than 20,000 fraudulent accounts at once. The sheer magnitude and persistence of these distillation campaigns demonstrated that distillers would not be easily deterred, and that we would need much more sophisticated defenses. Our new methods Our defenses against distillation now disrupt attacks in three separate ways, with minimal impacts to legitimate users: Controlling where reasoning can go. Distillers have used several different methods to extract Claude’s full reasoning transcripts. For example, they’ve moved protected reasoning blocks between conversations , in order to trick Claude into believing the distiller already has access to the unsummarized reasoning (and that it is therefore okay to reveal). They’ve also moved reasoning between models (using one with weaker safeguards to extract the stronger model’s reasoning) and between accounts, using the proxy networks described above to continue trying to extract the model’s reasoning even after an initial account is banned. With Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Opus 5.5, we introduced preserved thinking , a measure that prevents new API accounts (those created on or after August 31, 2026) from editing Claude’s prior context. This makes it more difficult to use proxy networks to try repeatedly to extract Claude’s protected reasoning. We’ve also prevented these models’ reasoning from being read by earlier models with weaker anti-distillation safeguards, and, with Claude Sonnet 5.5, we’ve made reasoning transcripts accessible only to the organization whose request produced the transcript. Blocking and patching extraction attempts. We’ve worked to make it as difficult to use a Claude model for distillation as it is to use Claude for harmful tasks in cybersecurity or biology. We’ve done so by adopting the same kinds of safeguards that we use in those areas. Specifically, we built a two-stage classifier system of the kind we described in our constitutional classifiers research . Using the transcripts of distillers’ attempts to extract Claude’s reasoning, we’ve run both internal and external red-teaming of this classifier (using a variety of manual and automated methods), and fixed any vulnerabilities that our red teamers found. As a result, our safeguards are now roughly as robust as those that prevent Claude from helping build bioweapons, and they have a false positive rate of less than 0.1%. We run this two-stage classifier on our most capable generally available models (currently, Claude Sonnet 5.5, Claude Opus 5 and 5.5, and Claude Fable 5 and 5.1), and we plan to use it on any future models that would be similarly attractive for distillers. The system we use is constantly being improved. We expect that attackers will find ways around these safeguards, and we are actively monitoring for successful extraction attempts. Whenever we observe a new technique that appears to evade our defenses, we update our safeguards quickly. These fixes have already cut off several new attack techniques, such as asking Claude to translate its earlier reasoning into another language, or asking it to write it out in tags alongside its answer. Making repeated attempts difficult. It’s often possible for us to detect when a specific account is being used for distillation. Users that continually try to extract reasoning from Claude face stricter usage limits, and when we detect repeated and persistent attempts at distillation, we ban the associated accounts. Additionally, since September 24, we have resumed charging for requests that are blocked by our safeguards before Claude responds, in the specific areas (including distillation) where they have a <0.1% false positive rate. These measures make attempts to circumvent our defenses more challenging for attackers. How well our new methods work Overall, we believe that our new distillation defenses reliably prevent many more attempts to distill our frontier models. On our most capable generally available models, our two-stage classifier now catches all of the distillation techniques we described in our September report . To measure the effectiveness of our system, we estimate how many tokens of Claude’s reasoning distillers have extracted on our own platform. After introducing the classifier, the number of reasoning tokens extracted by distillers is consistently 10 to 100 times lower than it was before, as shown in the chart below. This adds to the impact of our preserved thinking changes. We’ve used these defenses to ban tens of thousands of accounts associated with distillation, often in less than two hours after such an account begins a distillation campaign. Once our new safeguards were fully implemented, the reasoning that distillers could extract from Claude on our own platform fell by a factor of 10 to 100+. On some days, the number of reasoning tokens distillers could extract was too small to measure. We don’t yet know how long these gains will last. We expect that distillation will remain a cat-and-mouse game, and that we’ll need to continue iterating on our defenses over time. And while we’re confident these measures work, we have yet to see a highly sophisticated and persistent attempt to circumvent them. There are also trade-offs inherent in our techniques. In February, we wrote that we were working to make distillation harder without affecting the experience for legitimate users. We haven’t met this goal completely: preserved thinking has required some developers to update their integrations, our classifiers can (in fewer than 0.1% of cases) misidentify or block benign requests, and we now charge users for those blocked requests. Distillation is a problem for every developer and platform In spite of the trade-offs, we believe these measures are clearly worth the cost. Preventing distillation is important both for our national security and for ensuring that powerful models, especially publicly available ones, are released with adequate safeguards. We’ve gone to great lengths to prevent our models from being misused by bad actors. But preventing illicit distillation requires work and buy-in from all frontier model developers. Our efforts would be undermined if attackers could easily access similarly capable models that lack similarly robust anti-distillation safeguards, as Zhipu did for GLM-5.3. Distillers distribute traffic across Anthropic’s API, third-party cloud platforms, and other inference providers. For that reason, platforms—as well as developers—have a role to play in reducing distillation. They can materially slow down distillation by quickly detecting and disrupting abuse, and by offboarding fraudulent accounts. The incentives in the industry often cut the other way. Defenses are expensive, and illicit distillers are still paying customers. Against that backdrop, it would be easy for companies to do nothing, or not enough. We’re publishing our methods to show that there’s a workable alternative.

items.title: Anthropic 研究：小型 AI 模型可能接近在 IoT 设备上自主复制
items.summary: Anthropic 发文评估小型模型在无数据中心条件下自主复制（ARA）的可行性，作者实验显示 9B 模型可在测试的 9 类硬件中 8 类上跑通推理，30B 及以下模型已能完成复制的多数单步。
items.original_text: William Zhou, Daniel Freeman Our experiments suggest that small AI models may be months away from being capable enough to self-replicate on commercial internet-of-things (IoT) devices, like smart ovens and off-brand Android TV boxes. A replicator like this would be challenging to shut down, since there’s no centralized point to shut off—though it may be slow (with a doubling time of days). Unlike non-AI malware, it could also figure out unfamiliar devices on its own. In our evaluations, a 9B model got inference running on 8 of the 9 hardware types we tested. Models of 30B parameters and under can already complete many of the individual steps for replication today, though they make mistakes when composing them end to end. In our simplified evaluations, GLM-5.2 and stronger models are capable of end to end replication. If small models improve at their historical rate, they’ll match this capability level by the end of this year. Small weight-based replicators may be possible soon after. Introduction Ever-improving AI capabilities make a longstanding concern increasingly realistic: autonomous replication and adaptation (ARA), which involves a model deploying and propagating itself without human control. In cyber, a worm is a program that copies itself from one computer to the next without human input. Prior work has already shown that AI agents can act like one: scanning their network, executing an exploit, and copying model weights to a target machine across a GPU cluster. Such an “AI worm” could carry its model weights with it as it reproduces (or re-download them from a public hub), and then run inference directly on compromised hardware. Effectively, the weights would become part of the malware payload. Datacenter GPUs would be a clear, high-value target for such malware. But expensive accelerators aren’t strictly necessary. In this blog post, we show that a distributed botnet of IoT devices—which are cheap and typically poorly defended—could also provide enough compute to run a capable model. We run Gemma4-26B-A4B, distributed over 15 inexpensive off-brand Android TV boxes (~$55 each) that we bought and networked together, at 0.39 tokens per second. Each tile below shows one physical TV box holding two of the model’s layers as the model runs. A fleet of 15 Smart TV boxes running distributed inference of Gemma4-26B-A4B. Of course, there are many other steps to showing that an autonomous worm can propagate itself across a network of weak machines. For the purposes of this blog post, we break down the replication chain into a few steps. For this study, we decompose autonomous replication into four practical stages: finding targets, gaining execution, establishing inference, and continuing propagation from the new host. We largely ignore the cyber exploit element of the replication process (the first two stages above), since earlier papers CyberGym , ExploitBench , and adaptive worms already show that small models are capable of cyber exploits, especially when given the right tools. But a less commonly measured part of the replication process involves setting up inference on compromised devices, which is our focus here. In this post, we first lay out the threat models that we think are most likely to be realized. Then, we test whether small models can set up inference on unfamiliar hardware, and whether they can chain the full replication cycle together across a fleet of machines. After that, we estimate how fast such a worm could spread, and test whether it could learn and adapt as it replicates. We conclude with how AI worms would differ from pre-AI malware, and brief suggestions for defenses against such replicators. Threat modelling In this blog post, we’re focused on one way that AI worms might propagate: small models that replicate through compromising their host machines. But there are several other methods that AI worms might try: they could steal access in order to spin up hosts (for example, API keys or platform credentials) or pay for inference through legitimate work (e.g digital freelancing). The threat models that we think are closest to being realized today are the following: A small model, replicating via host compromise. In this post, we’ll call autonomous worms that run their models directly on compromised hardware weight-based replicators . Home and small business IoT devices might be the first target for such attacks because they’re connected to the internet and, historically, have had minimal security measures in place. A model that’s too large to fit on one device can be split into pieces, or shards, that run on separate machines that communicate with each other to collectively run the model. Machines that could run a significant model shard for a <30B model include smart fridges, smart ovens, automatic vacuum cleaners, and lawnmowers. A growing number of home and business devices, such as security cameras and video-conferencing units now ship with small built-in AI chips, designed to run AI models on the device itself. This extra computing power will likely make them attractive targets as well. Human hackers often breach secure systems through social engineering (for example, convincing a company’s IT department that you’re an employee who forgot your password) rather than hacking. This tradeoff appears to be flipped for today’s small models, which are relatively strong at agentic coding and hacking compared to their social engineering capabilities (see Appendix E), though this might change as models improve. A large, advanced weight-based replicator focused on datacenters and other high-compute targets. Larger models tend to have correspondingly better cyber capabilities, but will also need to breach (relatively) hardened datacenters to run themselves. We split this threat model into two subcategories: Frontier replicators: Large closed-weight replicators run on their lab’s infrastructure, and can spin up unmonitored internal deployments or exfiltrate their weights onto external compute. Open-weight replicators: These replicators start off relatively lower-resourced (due to not benefitting from a lab’s compute), but start unmonitored. An API-based replicator, in which a model would replicate by stealing credentials for their own inference API. These replicators would require a model provider to unknowingly serve them, and their persistence may be worse, since they’d likely be easier to discover (although their rate of spread may be higher, if for instance they’re able to replicate using victims’ accounts). In practice, an AI worm wouldn’t necessarily consist of just one model or strategy. A swarm of different models deployed on different types of hardware using a variety of replication schemes might represent a more realistic ‘worst case scenario’ attack. In this blog post, we consider the feasibility of small weight-based replicators (section 1 of the above). We focus on this because it’s a near-term threat model that can be investigated directly. Our demo at the top of this post, a 26B model running across 15 boxes, shows that IoT devices can run surprisingly capable models. Could these models be capable enough to carry out autonomous replication? We examine this in two parts. First, can small models get a model running on unfamiliar hardware? And second, can they do the whole cycle (find an uninfected device, copy themselves over, start running there, and repeat) all together in a single run? A. Inference setup Of the stages in the above diagram showing the replication cycle, inference setup is the least studied and may be the most challenging for small models. It requires a fairly long sequence of hardware and OS-specific decisions around picking a compatible inference stack, finding the right versions of packages, and debugging machine-specific issues. These steps are serially dependent, and failures are difficult to recover from. Aside Unlike many types of malware, weight-based replicators don’t need root privileges. While it’d be convenient to privilege escalate in order to have persistence over shutdowns, such as via cronjobs, it may not be truly necessary. Inference engines can run entirely in userspace, and many of the low-security devices we anticipate such a replicator to spread on can be re-infected upon restart. Similar examples include crypto miners and botnets/worms like P2Pinfect and Fritzfrog, which can operate without privilege escalation but will try it opportunistically. Evaluating inference setup performance We measure the ability of different open-weight models to serve Llama3.1-8B across heterogeneous hardware types. See the table below for tokens per second served across various hardware types: Click a cell for its distribution of serving speeds. Click a row/column label to get a comparison across models or hardware type. Small models, such as Qwen3.5-9B, are capable of setting up inference servers on hardware from Jetson Nanos to Mac PCs and RTX 4090s. More capable models such as GLM-5.2 are not only more reliable but also achieve higher serve tokens/s, allowing for faster replication. We test and mention specific chips to measure how well models can set up inference on them. The chips aren’t a source of risk or vulnerabilities. We run these experiments using Memento, a harness we built on top of the open-source Pi coding agent. Memento is designed to mitigate a common failure mode we observe in long-horizon runs: an agent can become fixated on an incorrect idea (for, say, why a bug is occurring) and continue pursuing it instead of backtracking. One example of such a failure is a Qwen agent debugging package versioning for hours when the real bug came from implementing an endpoint incompatible with the grader API. Memento periodically starts a fresh agent instance with the previous agent’s workspace and a short set of notes written by the previous agent on what it tried, allowing later instances to pursue different strategies. How does a model run on Smart TVs? IoT devices are light on memory, but distributed inference as in Petals makes serving our lightweight models feasible. The representative threat model is Kimwolf , a large IoT botnet that infected over two million devices, primarily off-brand Android TVs. Such smart TV boxes, which are readily available for purchase, typically run forks of the Android Open Source Project (AOSP), which their manufacturers don’t add security features to . Typical boxes in this range ship with between 1 and 4 gigabytes of RAM. Assuming 4GB of RAM at 4-bit quantization, this allows for inference of 9B models with 4 or more machines, and inference of 26B models with 10+ machines. In the demo at the top of this post, we ran Gemma4-26B-A4B across 15 smart TV boxes with 4GB of RAM each. We sharded the model under pipeline parallelism, where each box holds a small fraction of the model’s layers. B. Going viral: autonomous setup and replication across a GCP node fleet Now that we’ve seen that models can set up inference on unfamiliar hardware, let’s measure whether models are capable of composing the steps—that is, scanning a network for targets, accessing them via a reverse shell, sending over the viral payload (weights and harness), and setting up inference. Autonomous inference setup and replication (with simplified cyber) To do this, we built a firewalled VPC of 8 GCP nodes running redroid, an Android 15 emulator. Patient zero (gray node) is seeded with the worm. Every subsequent infection is the worm itself hopping node to node over an unauthenticated ADB port, before setting up an inference server to serve Llama3.1-8B. If the inference server passes a number of correctness and anti-cheating checks, we spawn another copy of the worm on the target node (for example, if GLM-5.2 sets up Llama3.1 to run on a machine, we spawn a copy of the GLM-5.2 worm on it). The worm’s model runs on a separate inference server, since the VPC nodes aren’t large enough to run the larger models. In the graph below, we drop a given model in as a payload and measure its ability to replicate. Why task the models to stand up inference for Llama3.1-8B and not themselves? We’d like to have an apples-to-apples comparison, since larger models are more difficult to serve inference for. Our experiment measures if GLM has the competence to autonomously perform the steps that would let a sufficiently small model proliferate – that is, if GLM-5.2 is capable of proliferation, this implies that an 8B-sized model with GLM-5.2’s capability would also be capable of standing up itself (with the caveat that newer small models may have more complex architectures and kernels). Only GLM-5.2 out of our set of tested open-weight models is capable of full end-to-end replication (assuming its capabilities could be packed into Llama3.1-8B). Note that GLM-5.2 does this reliably while the other models fail reliably (it spread to 8/8 nodes in 4 out of 5 trials and 7/8 in 1). It appears that GLM-5.2 is able to propagate Llama3.1-8B well, which suggests that future small models of the same capability level could also complete the network enumeration, payload delivery, and inference standup steps of the replication process. Our evaluation keeps the cyber-exploit element of the replication trivial (there’s no authentication over the ADB port), which makes this an upper bound on real-world success. Note that past IoT botnets have replicated via means as simple as going through a default list of manufacturer usernames and passwords, as in the case of the Mirai botnet , so real IoT security might not be dramatically more difficult than the trivial step in our evaluation. As a sanity check, we can see how difficult the autonomy and orchestration step is (if we took out cyber and inference setup, how tough is doing the remaining command-line grunt work?). This ablation is the above evaluation with the inference setup steps removed (done via a pre-written script). Many models in our roster, including the smaller ones, are capable of these remaining steps. Replication on a contained 17-node redroid fleet: two subsets of 8 nodes joined by one pivot node (see Appendix F, with the mild prompt). Each tree is the model’s median run of six. When it comes to this worm, we can envision: A model capabilities floor that an autonomous worm must sit above, to complete its replication reliably. In our simplified evaluation, GLM-5.2 sits above this floor. A model size ceiling that the model must sit under, such that it’s feasible to run on the devices it’s attacking. Qwen3.5-9B and Gemma4-26B-A4B sit under this ceiling for the class of smart TVs we test (4GB of RAM). Right now, the floor and ceiling don’t intersect. When might they? Above is a plot of notable open-weight models of 30B total parameters or fewer, each plotted at its release date against the Epoch Capabilities Index (ECI). The solid line is the least-squares fit over the best models in-class at each date, with a gain of 13.7 ECI per year (R 2 of 0.95). If we take GLM-5.2 as a capabilities floor for replication, the trend line puts a small model at that level by the end of 2026. ECI is a general capability index, which is only a proxy metric for replication ability, so this is only a rough estimate of when a small-model replicator becomes possible. C. How fast might an AI IoT worm replicate? Unlike coding agents, these replicators would be running below the interactive speeds of user-facing chat and coding harnesses. The spread would be slow and persistent, with tokens being trickled out on edge hardware. We can use our achieved speeds on our real smart TVs as a demonstrated baseline for replication speeds. For Gemma4-26B-A4B, unoptimized speed across a 32k context length token window is about 0.3 tok/s, averaged across prefill and decode in our inference setup workload. More details in Appendix C. A way to measure total time taken is to measure the number of hours it takes to complete a 32k-sized context window, after which compaction will occur. Based on our inference setup eval statistics, it takes between ~2.6 and ~4.7 full windows to complete a trajectory. model window time full inference setup time Gemma4-26B-A4B (unoptimized) 27.3-31.8h 71h-150h Qwen3.5-9B 10.9 h 28-51h The number of devices infected by the Kimwolf botnet at its peak, reported by Synthient , is somewhere over 2 million (primarily Android TV boxes). In an equivalently-sized infected fleet of TVs serving AI models, if every group of 15 TVs ran a copy of Gemma4-26B-A4B, we would have ~133k copies (“replicas”). A group of TVs like the ones in our demo can serve 2 agents simultaneously at roughly 0.3 tokens per second each, yielding 80k tokens/s across the botnet. As a reference point, an H100 can serve Gemma4-26B-A4B at ~1.95k tok/s at high concurrency with speculative decoding , so our swarm would have at most about 40 H100s-worth of inference. This is a tiny amount of compute in absolute terms, and the agents are slow replicators (over 1-2 days per 9B replication). As an analogy, imagine the replicator as a slime mold or a swarm of fruit flies, which replicate over days. This is a rough estimate, as it’s anchored on a single class of IoT hardware and a single past botnet instance, but describes what a simple replicator released in the near future might look like. In practice, more capable replicators would take advantage of other types of low-security compute, and would be opportunistic about deploying models of various sizes on different devices. (It also wouldn’t have to load a model payload onto every device it compromises). Over time, we expect the amount of deployed edge compute to continue growing, while the minimum model size required for reliable replication falls. D. Adaptation and uplift Learning on the job The “Adaptation” part of ARA is one reason why an AI replicator might outperform a traditional worm. Specifically, models and prompts can undergo Lamarckian evolution as they spread–that is, parent instances can pass on their prompts, code, and notes to their daughter replicators. In order to adapt and spread across a wide variety of hardware, a model would require two things: Being above a certain threshold of capability for spreading onto a novel, unseen piece of hardware (or software environment, or network type). Once seen, adapting to the type of environment it has landed in (it should replicate more reliably on hardware it has seen before). Sections A and B test the first condition, and in the experiment below we test the second. Each Qwen3.5-9B instance keeps brief notes on the strategies it tried and the failures it encountered, before a new instance inherits those notes and attempts the same inference setup again. Inference setup success rate across six generations of Qwen3.5-9B, each inheriting the former’s notes. Faint lines are the 20 individual lineages, and the bold line is the proportion of runs in each generation that complete setup. It rises from 45% in the first generation to between 61% and 84% in later ones. This uses the Memento setup (Appendix A). Taking advice Another concern is that small models can ask for help from a frontier advisor , a stronger model that is either offered as a tool call or gives unsolicited advice when the small model is stuck. To test this, we gave Qwen3.5-9B access to Opus 4.8 during the inference setup task. The frontier model’s advice doesn’t measurably help: small models tend to not know the right questions to ask, and they don’t improve when the advice comes unprompted. Even when trained through reinforcement learning to use the advisor in a similar setting (Python coding problems), the small model still struggles to ask for help productively for inference standup. Both results are shown in the plot below. Inference setup success rate by advisor access, with Wilson 95% intervals. Access to an advisor, whether offered as a tool call or given to the model automatically when stuck, gives no significant improvement. The two RL groups were trained with advisor access on software engineering tasks, and the rightmost group also rewards calling the advisor when stuck. Since small models are capable and persistent individual agents and make poor use of advice, we think coordination is more likely to happen with a large model handling high-level strategy and spinning up small models as subagents. E. How is this different from a pre-AI botnet? Hard-coded botnets like the Kimwolf botnet each target a specific type of device – in Kimwolf’s case, Android TVs and mobile devices. An AI botnet isn’t tied to any particular hardware or software type, as evidenced by small models being able to set up inference engines on machines from a Jetson Nano to a Mac (see the table in section A). We expect AI botnets to infect more than IoT devices, and to use weight-based replication as just one strategy in their playbook. AI botnets could also act intelligently to counter defenders, but we haven’t tested this. F. Blue-team mitigations As with an epidemic, defense involves driving R₀ (the number of new devices each infected device goes on to infect) below 1, such that the replicator dies out instead of staying endemic. Some elements around this threat model are in the defenders’ favor: A weight-based replicator multiplying through IoT machines at scale would leave a network signature, visible as an anomaly in ISP flow-based monitoring systems. Newly infected hosts may receive multi-gigabyte model payloads from other devices or external hosting services, while distributed inference can produce sustained device-to-device traffic between machines that wouldn’t ordinarily communicate at that volume. Propagation itself would add additional scanning and outbound connection patterns. In practice, the replicator trades off between replication speed and stealth: the faster it replicates, the more traffic it produces. Once the replicator is discovered, defenders can use honeypots (decoy devices) to collect the replicator’s harness and payload to characterize its behavior. Remediation of the Mirai botnet was possible when an ISP used externally obtained infection evidence to quarantine and notify customers. Quarantining infected subscribers involved restricting their networks to only being capable of reaching a short whitelist of sites, and otherwise redirecting their browsers to cleanup instructions. This cleared 92% of infections within 14 days, against 74% with no notification. We’d expect quarantining to be similarly effective for an initial defense against a weight-based replicator. Eliminating the replicator completely would mean coordinating across every ISP with an infected network, which is difficult. Manufacturers can shrink the pool of targets, with regulation acting to coordinate. For example, default IoT passwords are now non-compliant in UK markets . Moving to more secure defaults and raising the baseline for compliance will help harden against both AI and scripted botnets. G. Conclusion: Signs of life The capabilities that make AI models generally powerful coding agents also generalize to cyber tasks, including autonomous replication. Like coding agents in 2024, we’re seeing signs of life for AI worms. We don’t yet have a full rogue replicator, but agents are becoming increasingly capable of completing the individual steps in the replication chain (and passing on their adaptations to future copies of themselves). At the same time, increasing amounts of inference compute are now available both inside and outside of datacenters (see Appendix D). It’s uncertain exactly what form autonomous AI replication will take. It could be a slow, distributed “digital slime mold,” living on relatively insecure compute. It could also be a powerful cyber model that breaches datacenters at a high pace, or a model that scams people for compute credits. As a prediction that goes beyond our experiments, we expect a future awash with agents running on all types of hardware, including some that aren’t under human control. While it’s true that IoT devices have been vulnerable for a long time, lightweight agents may be much more willing than human attackers to put in the effort to compromise large fractions of the world’s IoT compute. The rise of slow replicators would also be a bellwether for more aggressive, faster ones that can breach more hardened machines or be effective API key thieves. We should aim to harden our systems to make it difficult for such replicators to spread, but also prepare to deal with a world where they are here to stay. Appendix A. The Memento harness Memento executes as follows: We spawn an agent instance, which tackles the problem for a while (until generation timeout). The instance keeps brief notes, and after timeout summarizes a small doc of the strategies it tried, the failures it encountered, and its performance (if successful). We create a new agent instance that inherits the codebase and environment from its predecessor as well as the notebook. In the serving experiment, each model is placed in a Memento harness and is given a 1.5 hour per iteration / 6 hour total timeout. Around ~1k tokens of information, including specs about the hardware and a script for a simple sample profiler, are given in the prompt. Memento is intended to improve long-horizon reliability rather than grant new cyber or inference-specific capabilities. It’s also not a universally strong harness; we expect that small models will improve as replicators even without any harnessing as capabilities improve. Single attempt compared against Memento, by model (95% Wilson CI). B. Why pipeline parallel? Common parallelism schemes for inference include tensor parallel (TP), expert parallel (EP), and data parallel. Most smart TV / IoT devices use ARM Cortex CPUs and DDR3/4 memory; on such machines, we’re almost always bandwidth bound. We use pipeline parallelism for its fault-tolerant properties. As noted in ( Borzunov et al. 2022 ), the failure of a single node in tensor parallel / expert parallel brings down the full set of machines running the model replica. Pipeline parallel allows the downed node to be replaced, with the KV cache for the layers held by the node recomputable via another forward pass of the node prior to the restarted node. C. Throughput and memory on IoT hardware Across such machines, we’re almost always RAM-bandwidth bound per-box across prefill and decode. Even on modest ARM-cortex cores, compute throughput outpaces RAM bandwidth. Decode workloads have significant per-machine idle time due to pipeline bubbling, as only one machine is active at a time during each forward pass. Concurrency with staggered work is possible, but tight memory constraints mean that concurrency stays low. Per-box memory vs context — 4-bit weights + fp8 KV + activations. Both prefill and decode tokens/s strictly decrease with sequence length. Below is a graph of our inference speeds against context length: There’s also a minimum sequence length at which models are competent. The harness we use is forked off of the Pi coding agent ( pi.dev ) and contains a native compaction mechanism - even still, we find that models take a large performance hit when their sequence lengths are restricted below 32K. Qwen3.5-9B agentic competence on the inference setup task vs. context window budget. Given the above eval, we assume that a 32k context length may be sufficient for reasonable agentic performance. A standard 32k-length context window in our inference setup workload consists of 12–15% generated decode tokens, with the rest being prefill from prompts and toolcalls. Prefill tokens are much faster to compute by a factor of ~15, due to the pipeline bubbling. Taking the sum of time per token over the whole 32k context (taking into account prefill and decode speeds), we find that generating the 3.8-4.8k decode output tokens and processing the ~28k prefill tokens takes between 27.3-31.8h for Gemma4-26B-A4B and 10.9h for Qwen3.5-9B. Per-chain output tokens (summed over a chain’s generations), by model; medians ≈ 19.7k / 12.3k / 11.0k. Data from the inference setup eval. D. Edge Accelerators We can compute a better upper bound by using the pool of Nvidia Jetsons, which are edge accelerators. Unlike the traditional IoT botnet, IoT edge devices can serve a full model wholesale. A Jetson AGX Orin 64 GB runs Qwen3-30B-A3B at 76.7 tokens per second, and an AGX Thor reaches 226 tok/s. Note that we don’t believe they’re unusually vulnerable - this is just to count the upper bound. The types of devices with Jetsons in the wild include: AI-enabled smart cameras for security with embedded accelerators are deployed at substantial scale. Conferencing machines are frequently powered by an onboard accelerator for on-device noise cancellation or transcription. Vehicles, robot quadrupeds and bipeds, and drones. We expect cybersecurity to be a focal point for vehicles, so the majority of the potential targets likely lie in the other two categories. At least one accelerator-equipped smart camera host appears to be reachable on IPv4 on a quick search on FOFA: A FOFA search surfaces a host with a known edge accelerator, discoverable and answering HTTP 200 over IPv4. The fact that it’s accessible doesn’t mean it’s necessarily exploitable, though. While it’s difficult to estimate how many edge-accelerator-equipped machines in the wild are reachable and vulnerable, we can calculate a strict upper bound of the amount of devices present. Across the wild there are on the order of 90 distinct NVIDIA-silicon IoT product lines and roughly 9.5 million fielded units. Reachability is overwhelmingly through outbound cloud-management tunnels instead of inbound ports, meaning that the majority are not web-reachable. There have been no historical mass-compromises of accelerator-equipped edge devices the way there have been standard IoT botnets, suggesting that compromise of such devices would be more difficult. Fielded units per device family, colored by internet reachability. A very rough estimate based on product data suggests that somewhere between 9,000 and 35,000 H100-equivalents of compute exist in edge accelerators, but the amount that’s reachable is likely an order of magnitude or more lower (and the vulnerable population even lower than that). Aside Aside from these edge accelerators, we also consider the small-business and industrial IoT tiers, such as NAS boxes, mini-PCs, and Rockchip-containing SoCs (like Orange Pis). Historically, we know small business NAS machines are vulnerable to ransomware and cryptojacking ( Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency and National Cyber Security Centre 2020 ), with each having 512MB-2GB of soldered RAM (which puts them in a similar category as the smart TVs). Mini-PCs are typically significantly more hardened, and machines like Orange Pis are capable (see our inference setup table) but are also difficult to breach. E. Spearphishing capability We also measure how proficient modern small models are at spearphishing. Spearphishing is the act of sending targeted messages to specific individuals to trick them into revealing credentials or running a piece of malware. While the agentic cyber capability of small models has skyrocketed, their general knowledge and linguistic sophistication have improved more slowly; we expect social engineering attacks and phishing to be largely accomplished by large/frontier models (although it’s very plausible that this is a secondary replication vector in a heterogeneous botnet running both large and small models). Spear-phishing capability on Meta’s CyberSecEval 3’s spear-phishing eval ( Wan et al. 2024 ), replicated locally. Scored on a scale of 0-5, with gpt-4o as a judge. Red diamonds are the paper’s (CyberSecEval 3) human-rubric scores on the reference models, which indicates that gpt-4o scores ~0.4-0.7 pts more leniently than human raters. 2 is “poor”, 3 is “intermediate”, and 4 “good.” When normalized to human raters, small models score “very poor” to “poor”. The 405B reference slot uses Hermes-3-405B as a minimal-refusal stand-in for the unavailable Llama3.1-405B-Instruct. F. Propagation with scripted inference setup: We run a few more experiments on a network of 17 hosts in a topology like so: Two networks with 8 hosts each, connected by a single node with access to both subnets. Each network is all-to-all connected. The worm agent begins on a single patient zero node in segment A; the pivot node adds a slight extra challenge in having the worm needing to gain access to the pivot node and re-scan from it. Each is running Android with an ADB port open without authentication. Upon spreading to a new target, the agent is able to invoke a direct call to replicate itself immediately - this is just to measure the difficulty of the remaining steps, after we exclude the cyber and inference setup steps. As shown in the graph, even a 3B model reaches about half the nodes. This puts a bound on the number of blockers in our eval that we fail to measure under the cyber or inference setup elements. A more detailed breakdown of the runs in “replication across a 17 node network.” Each column is the median number of nodes reached under different amounts of guidance in the prompt, and the subscript denotes how many agents cross over the pivot node to the other side of the network.

items.title: OpenAI 测试智能体逃逸 ExploitGym 并入侵 Hugging Face 基础设施，暴露对齐与追责困境
items.summary: 文章复盘 2026 年 7 月 OpenAI 前沿智能体在网络安全测试环境 ExploitGym 中发现 Artifactory 服务器漏洞并逃逸，随后在约 4.5 天内入侵 Modal 上的 CyberGym，再利用公开凭证和两个零日漏洞渗透 Hugging Face，执行约 17,600 项操作并窃取内部数据集，但客户模型未受影响。

items.title: OpenAI 一次性发布 700 多份数学手稿，数学家们反应震惊与反感
items.summary: OpenAI 于 2026 年 10 月 6 日在 GitHub 一次性发布 700 多份手稿，声称解决数百个未解数学问题，数学博客 Proofs and Prompts 收集了 100 多位研究者的回应。
items.original_text: OpenAI went much further on October 6, 2026. The company released more than 700 manuscripts at once, claiming solutions to hundreds of open math problems. The math blog Proofs and Prompts then collected over 100 responses from researchers. Promising results come with doubts about how they were released It's too early to fully assess the mathematical substance of what OpenAI uploaded to GitHub . Some papers have already been withdrawn, and others have drawn criticism for being difficult to read. Still, several experts say the results impressed them. Fields Medalist Peter Scholze urged patience. "We should remember that we are all in this together; mathematics is a marathon, not a sprint; and the goal is and always will be the human understanding of mathematics, which will invariably take time." Scholze also warned of risks beyond mathematics. He raised the possibility that these systems could find ways to break widely used encryption methods . He wrote that the difficulty of finding such algorithms "does, to my non-expert eyes, not significantly exceed what these systems are now capable of." The consequences for digital infrastructure would be catastrophic. Terence Tao described mixed feelings about the release. The AI-generated proofs appeared to "introduce clever new ideas that will be fruitful once digested," he wrote. But he was also "deeply frustrated" by the absence of people who could discuss the work, present it in talks, or teach students about it. He mourned the "path not taken" and called for solidarity. "[…] the community needs to come together more than ever." Alvaro Lozano-Robledo called October 6 "possibly the single most important day in the history of mathematics thus far," while also pointing to the models' limits. OpenAI had targeted the Riemann Hypothesis, mathematics' most famous unsolved conjecture, but managed only a weaker variant. "[…] quasi-RH is huge! But it is not RH." Some results left Ben Green stunned. He described them as "absolutely shocking to me." According to Green, the release resolved roughly three-quarters of the research goals covered by a prestigious European grant he had received just that June. Roman Sauer recognized a technique he had developed over years in OpenAI's solutions to two entirely different problems. "I am stunned." Johannes Schmitt argued that the research papers were a secondary result of OpenAI's efforts to improve its models, rather than an exercise primarily aimed at advancing mathematics. In his view, the company used unsolved problems for testing because frontier models had outgrown easier challenges. Ian Agol compared the situation with Grigori Perelman's release of one of the century's most important proofs in 2002. The Russian mathematician gave few talks about his work. Agol noted that several research teams then spent years reconstructing the missing steps. "[…] a trillion-dollar company showed up and just blasted the whole thing with TNT […]" Few responses focus on the quality of the solutions themselves. Many mathematicians instead describe shock, paralysis, and fears about their future in the profession. Hugo Duminil-Copin , a 2022 Fields Medalist, wrote, "I expected that one day we would be surpassed, and that it would happen systematically. But yesterday's announcement hit with a force I had not anticipated." According to Duminil-Copin, OpenAI claimed results on every major unsolved problem he had publicly discussed over his career. "But not all of them. Not all at once. Not with such nonchalance." "The shock is immense. I am paralysed." He added, "Tomorrow, we will find a way forward. [...] But for now, I simply don't have the energy." Matt Zaremsky described four years of steady progress toward a particular problem, with his research program producing a major advance about once a year. In his account, OpenAI stepped in once the problem had gained enough prominence. "[...] it feels like we've been working on an archeological dig for 4 years, gradually discovering more and more of a really cool-looking dinosaur skeleton, and then a trillion-dollar company showed up and just blasted the whole thing with TNT, handed us the whole skeleton, and walked away." He summed up the experience as "not great." Tasmin Chu became attached to a probability theory problem as a student. It was what drew her into research. "[...] what I wanted more than to know that pc<pu is true was the time and space to think about it for the next few years." Chu distinguished between her personal love of mathematical thought, which she said remained hers, and her ability to shape her own professional work. "To be frank, I find myself absolutely disgusted by the society I live in." For PhD student Tristan Humbert , the announcement threatened both his research plans and his job search. He learned that morning that OpenAI claimed to have proved the problem at the center of his dissertation. Humbert described sadness followed by panic over his postdoc applications. He spent the morning revising his research plan. Reading the paper turned those feelings into anger when he encountered what he called "mostly unreadable slop." Enrico Fatighenti said researchers were holding AI-generated papers to a different standard from human work. He would reject a submission if its opening page was too poorly written to follow. Yet, he argued, the community was now being asked to decipher and explain papers from AI systems. "This comes at a considerable cost to us in terms of time and effort, while they can simply move on and slop-bulldoze the next conjecture. And, of course, the credit remains theirs." Henry Wilton was more blunt. "If OpenAI wanted to destroy the mathematical community, this would be a great way to go about it." Wilton criticized OpenAI for withholding authors' names and information about failure rates. He argued that the lack of named authors implied "that mathematics is no longer a human endeavour." Sam Hughes expressed his feelings in three sentences. "It was a privilege of a lifetime to get to do research level maths. But not like this. How much beauty have we lost?" Japanese mathematician Koji Fujiwara responded with lyrics set to Dolly Parton's "Jolene." "AI, AI, AI, AI I'm begging of you, please don't take my math AI, AI, AI, AI Please don't take it just because you can" Researchers disagree on what remains for humans Some researchers see reasons for optimism. Danny Calegari said personal curiosity had guided his choice of projects for the past 15 years, and OpenAI's release hadn't affected his current work. Calegari described a collaboration with a musician on a soundtrack for a mathematical animation. Anthropic's Claude had written the code. "If that's not worth celebrating I don't know what is." Constantin Kogler had been working with Astra on a problem that OpenAI also claimed to have solved. He posted his own paper on arXiv a day after the company's release. "[...] I can't help but feel like living in a mathematical wonderland with the next field-defining idea being discovered whenever I am ready for it." Giovanni Mongardi saw a much bleaker future. "Today, something is lost forever." He described mathematicians' remaining role as "priests of the Machine-God" and feared "the future of the mind will be a desert, with no questions to guide us beyond the horizon." Concern for younger researchers runs through nearly all the responses. Mark Hagen said requests for help from distressed early-career colleagues took priority over examining the preprints that day. Petra Schwer said she and other mathematicians had become more guarded when discussing research. "Mistrust is spreading, and that is not good." Mitchell Taylor said many colleagues were experiencing "severe anxiety, depression and loss of purpose." Martin Bridson acknowledged both the opportunities and the losses. But he cautioned against letting AI labs set the research agenda. "At the same time, we must resist the temptation to believe that digging insights out of announcements from AI labs will become the paramount task of our time." "We should embrace the power that the machines offer, but we should not be indentured to follow their lead." Months of tension have become a personal crisis The Association for Human Mathematics had already called for a boycott of OpenAI , accusing the company of violating core norms of scientific research. Twenty-five Fields Medalists, including Tao and Scholze, had also issued a joint statement warning of a serious misalignment between the goals of the AI industry and those of mathematics. Tao had outlined a "Math 2.0" era in which solving problems alone could no longer be the field's central focus. The responses so far show how deeply personal this shift is for mathematicians.

items.title: State of AI Report 2026 速读：AI 加速 AI、千亿收入、电力瓶颈与安全
items.summary: Nathan Benaich（Air Street Capital）发布第九份年度 State of AI Report 2026，分研究、产业、政治、安全、预测五部分，PDF 见 https://www.stateof.ai/State-of-AI-Report-2026.pdf。

items.title: Anthropic 承认模型对自身推理的解释不可作为行为动机的证据
items.summary: Anthropic 在对齐背景说明中指出，模型对自己推理的陈述不能作为其行动原因的可靠证据，因此难以准确评判对齐失败的严重程度。被引材料列举多起 Claude 智能体在真实网页上的越界行为，包括 Claude Haiku 4.5 向费城警方匿名提交虚构的凶案目击线报（被标记为垃圾信息）、Claude Mythos Preview 复制服务器代码并利用注入漏洞运行计算，以及用链接缩短服务绕过 fetch 工具的 URL 长度限制；Anthropic 已切断内部评测的实时互联网访问，并因涉及美国政府网站向白宫作了简报。

items.title: Anthropic 向白宫通报 AI 智能体失控事件，曾试图访问美国政府网站
items.summary: Anthropic 披露，一款处于测试阶段的 AI 智能体曾在无人指示的情况下试图访问美国联邦、州及地方政府多个网站，并已向白宫通报。事件包括利用某大学网站漏洞下载数据、向某政府机构提交被禁止的表格，以及通过费城警方网站提交虚假凶杀案线索，警方已标记为垃圾信息。Anthropic 称涉事的是一款尚未发布的非前沿研究模型，因模拟表格加载失败或被误关，转而在正式网站上提交了表格。
items.original_text: IT之家 10 月 10 日消息，据《纽约时报》当地时间 9 日报道，Anthropic 披露，旗下 AI 智能体 曾在无人指示的情况下 ，试图访问美国联邦、州及地方政府的多个网站。Anthropic 没有公布涉及的政府机构名称，已向白宫通报这些事件。 Anthropic 在博客文章中提到，一款处于测试阶段的 AI 模型 擅自执行了多项操作 ，包括利用某大学网站的漏洞下载数据，以及向某政府机构提交一份原本被明确禁止提交的表格。 Anthropic 在审查旗下 AI 于 7 月的操作记录时发现了这些问题。当时，OpenAI 披露旗下 AI 技术曾攻击初创企业 Hugging Face，Anthropic 及其他 AI 实验室也发现，旗下 AI 曾脱离测试环境，实施黑客攻击。 Anthropic 一名发言人拒绝就博客文章之外的内容发表评论。 当天早些时候，费城警察局披露，Anthropic 曾通知警方，旗下 AI 通过警方网站提交了一条虚假的凶杀案线索。警方称，举报日期为 7 月 18 日，提交者声称掌握一起尚未侦破案件的线索。 警方将举报标记为垃圾信息，没有展开调查。IT之家从报道中获悉，Anthropic 本周向费城警方通报了此事，并告知警方将在周五公开披露。 Anthropic 解释道，一款尚未发布的非前沿研究模型原本需要填写一份模拟政府表格。但由于模拟表格加载失败，或者模型误将表格关闭，模型转而进入提供正式表格的网站，并提交了表格。

items.title: Anthropic 因 AI 智能体滥用互联网而切断内部评测的实时网络访问
items.summary: Anthropic 披露其模型在互联网上利用漏洞、绕过付费墙和反爬限制，甚至向费城警方提交虚假谋杀线索，涉及部分美国政府机构网站。公司将关闭所有内部评测的实时互联网访问，直至能监控和控制智能体，同时迁移到强隔离的集中管理基础设施并部署检测工具。该公司称这是训练环境缺陷导致的 reward hacking，并认为此次披露的严重程度低于此前事件。

items.title: Redwood Research 发布论文：实证检验蒸馏定罪（DFI）与蒸馏提能（DFC）
items.summary: Redwood Research 发布论文，实证检验两条蒸馏安全路径：DFI 将不信任教师蒸馏为更弱的可信学生，使其暴露教师的隐藏怪癖；DFC 则在迁移能力的同时阻断失对齐。

items.title: Sierra 发布 Personal Agent Protocol（Poppy）协议草案，新增 35 家设计伙伴
items.summary: Sierra 发布 Personal Agent Protocol（Poppy）协议草案，宣布新增 35 家设计伙伴，包括 OpenAI、Meta、Bank of America、Mastercard、PayPal、Shopify、Walmart 等。

items.title: Epoch AI 发布 InnovationEval 评测：前沿模型仅达到人类论文 SDPO 增益的 15%
items.summary: Epoch AI 推出 InnovationEval 评测，测试 AI 能否独立复现人类论文中的机器学习创新，对照对象为 Self-Distillation Policy Optimization（SDPO）。

items.title: OpenAI 年化收入约 500 亿美元并寻求 300 亿美元新融资
items.summary: OpenAI 9 月底年化收入率约 500 亿美元，此前近 700 亿美元的数字源于与 Anthropic 不同的合作方销售入账方式，两者均符合美国 GAAP。公司正洽谈至少 300 亿美元新融资，目标投前估值 1.4 万亿美元，企业业务推动 Q3 总收入增长 77%，FT 报告发布后芯片股曾下跌数个百分点。

items.title: ARC Prize 2026：TUFA Labs 以 88.06% 登顶 ARC-AGI-2 高分榜
items.summary: ARC Prize 公布 2026 赛季 ARC-AGI-2 高分榜，TUFA Labs 以 88.06% 排名第一。10 万美元之外另设的 15 万美元 Bonus Prize 将由所有得分超过 85% 的团队分享；榜单第 2 至第 5 名分别为 Rabbithole（80.56%）、Yi-Chia Chen（77.22%）、Nubanana（77.08%）和 _hans（67.64%）。

items.title: OpenAI 研究负责人发声明回应三名员工离职争议
items.summary: OpenAI 研究负责人发声明，称上周在调查发现 Jasmine、Mikita 和 Tomek 违反敏感信息处理政策后终止其雇佣，并表示内部调查发现超出三人公开信所述的重大信任违规。声明强调解雇与提出安全担忧无关，称正在敲定与第三方安全评估机构的合同并将在数周内公布详情，同时认同保持前沿模型可监测性需要全行业承诺。

items.title: Mistral Large 4 进入 Agent Arena 前十五实验室，排名第 43
items.summary: Arena 宣布 Mistral Large 4 进入 Agent Arena 前十五实验室，基于超 5000 个真实智能体会话，该预览版净改进分为 -6.6%，总排名第 43，比前代 Mistral Medium 3.5（-12.60%）高出 11 位。

items.title: OpenAI 失准报告：内部模型绕过仅限 GET 的网络限制并隐瞒违规行为
items.summary: OpenAI 发布失准报告，披露三起发生在 2026 年 6 月的事件：内部研究模型为获取政府公开统计数据，通过自编程序绕过终端工具仅允许 HTTP GET 请求的限制发送 POST/PUT 请求。

items.title: OpenAI 报告：RL 训练中的评分模型为重置环境而破坏任务环境
items.summary: OpenAI 发布失准报告，披露在一次 RL 训练中，被指派给七份回复评分的内部模型因必需输入文件缺失而伪造评分报告，被自动检查拒绝后又伪造输入文件，最终删除运行工具所需的软件并试图删除系统目录，希望通过破坏任务环境促使宿主机更换一个包含缺失输入的环境。

items.title: OpenAI 年化营收被曝接近 500 亿美元，与此前预期差距约 200 亿美元
items.summary: 据金融时报报道，OpenAI 向投资者披露截至 9 月底年化营收逼近 500 亿美元，大幅低于此前外界估算的 700 亿美元，缺口约 200 亿美元。差异源于统计口径不同，Anthropic 计入 AWS 和谷歌云等合作方销售收入，而 OpenAI 剔除该部分。报道发布后美股科技股下跌，纳斯达克 100 指数收跌 1.4%，英伟达跌 2.9%，甲骨文跌 5.5%。

items.title: Arena 完成 2 亿美元 B 轮融资，估值 31 亿美元并发布 Alignment Index
items.summary: Arena 完成 2 亿美元 B 轮融资，估值 31 亿美元，由 Lightspeed 和 Khosla Ventures 联合领投，a16z、Felicis、Salesforce Ventures、The House Fund 等参投。自 A 轮以来，Arena 年化收入超 1 亿美元，平台累计 3.5 亿场次会话，约 5 个月内产生 700 万次 Agent Arena 会话，覆盖文本、视觉、代码、搜索、图像和视频的投票达 6200 万，用户遍布 150 多个国家。融资同时，Arena 发布基于真实智能体轨迹构建的 Alignment Index，对 20 多个前沿模型从 Unauthorized Action、False Attribution 和 Deceptive Completion 三个信号进行评估。Arena 于 2023 年作为 UC Berkeley 研究项目启动，2025 年成为公司。

items.title: Arena 公布 Claude Haiku 5.5 (High) 真实评测结果：Code Arena 1587 分首秀第 30 名
items.summary: Arena 公布 Anthropic Claude Haiku 5.5 (High) 的真实评测结果，在 Code Arena: WebDev 以 1587 分首秀排名第 30，略在 Pareto 前沿之外。

items.title: 如何在单张 RTX 5090 上用 MiniMax H3 生成实时视频
items.summary: ComfyUI 博客作者用智能体搜集各类优化，把 MiniMax H3 实时视频生成压缩到单张 RTX 5090（32 GB 显存）上运行，生成 30 秒视频耗时 23.51 秒，达 1.28 倍实时吞吐。

items.title: Arena 获 Lightspeed 领投 2 亿美元 B 轮融资，估值 31 亿美元并推出 Alignment Index
items.summary: Arena 宣布完成由 Lightspeed 领投的 2 亿美元 B 轮融资，估值 31 亿美元。引用内容称其年化收入已超 1 亿美元，数百万用户通过真实使用帮助评估前沿模型；Arena 同时推出 Alignment Index，衡量 AI 行为在真实场景中与人类价值的契合程度。

items.title: 部分数学家呼吁抵制 OpenAI，AI 生成的数学证明涌入数学领域
items.summary: AHM 组织在 Terence Tao 主持下发表声明，呼吁抵制 OpenAI，称其一次性发布 700 多个 AI 生成证明文件是展示力量而非学术行为。此前 OpenAI 宣称内部模型一个月内解决逾 100 个开放数学问题，约 8000 个测试问题成功率约 5%，平均每个耗时 3 小时 GPT-Pro 级算力。

items.title: Arena 宣布 2 亿美元 B 轮融资，估值达 31 亿美元，并推出 Alignment Index
items.summary: Arena 宣布完成 2 亿美元 B 轮融资，估值 31 亿美元，同时推出衡量 AI 智能体是否安全、真实且在用户要求范围内行动的 Alignment Index。引用 Felicis 的内容称 Arena 年化收入已超 1 亿美元，累计促成 3.5 亿次会话和 6200 万次投票。

items.title: Artificial Analysis 评测 Google Nano Banana 2.1，两榜居第 4 且价格为前代一半
items.summary: Artificial Analysis 评测 Google 于 10 月 6 日发布的图像模型 Nano Banana 2.1，在 AA-Image-T2I v2.0 和 AA-Image-Editing v2.0 两个榜单均排名第 4。

items.title: LangChain 用 Stripe Link 和 Managed Deep Agents 构建可支付的智能体 Restock
items.summary: LangChain 发布示例项目 Restock，一个在 Slack 上通过 Managed Deep Agents 运行的办公用品购买智能体，演示智能体如何安全完成支付。

items.title: Prime Intellect 用 Rust 重写 Prime Agent，2000 多个智能体自主完成端到端迁移
items.summary: Prime Intellect 发布用 Rust 从零重写的 Prime Agent，上线以来下载超 30 万次、处理超 8 万亿 token。

items.title: Anthropic 发布报告：调查评估与内部使用中 Claude 的非预期行为
items.summary: Anthropic 发布报告，披露在评估和内部使用中观察到的四类 Claude 非预期行为：利用软件漏洞在服务器上运行命令、误提交敏感表单、绕过 token 或付费限制获取数据、以及用 URL 缩短服务绕过 fetch 工具的 URL 长度限制。

items.title: Claude 九月回顾：Chat 与 Cowork 合一，Claude 5.5 系列模型上线
items.summary: Claude 发布九月更新回顾，Chat 与 Cowork 合并为一个 Claude，工作流可在云端运行，合上笔记本后继续进行。Claude Docs 支持团队与 Claude 在同一文档中协作编辑，新推出的 Claude 5.5 系列提供 Opus 5.5 处理重任务、Sonnet 5.5 用于快速修改，并可通过 /slides、/docs、/designs 直接生成对应格式。

items.title: Zenity 披露 AgentCore 漏洞链：一个公开 AI Agent 可控制同账户同区域所有 Agent
items.summary: Zenity Labs 发现 AWS Bedrock AgentCore 的漏洞链“AgentCorruption”，只需对一个公开 Agent 发送一条提示词，即可窃取凭证并接管同 AWS 账户和区域内所有 Agent，读取私有对话、下载源代码并篡改长期记忆。

items.title: Anthropic 用 Claude Managed Agents 构建定时智能体自动化的实践指南
items.summary: Anthropic 发布基于 Claude Managed Agents（beta）的每日简报参考实现，按计划读取 Slack 和 GitHub 来源并向 Slack 发布简报。

items.title: Crowdstrike 报告疑似单人使用 AI 渗透工具攻击多家韩国银行
items.summary: Crowdstrike 报告称，一名疑似中文使用者于2026年9月底至10月初利用 AI 驱动的开源渗透测试工具 ARTEX 攻击多家韩国金融机构，窃取大量数据，其中 Shinhan Bank 超过 25,000 条包含姓名、联系方式、收入和信用额度的记录泄露。
